Recursive Industrial Intelligence

r4.0 · July 2026

Leonardo Stern · Independent researcher

A self-sustaining, self-expanding space industrial system is coherent as an argument; whether it is feasible or economical is a question for models. This paper combines the executed models with an explicit autonomous seed, its knowledge package, its material flows, and the dynamics by which it attempts to expand operating capacity.

Status. r4.0 release candidate, completed 2026-07-27 and not yet represented as an immutable tag or version DOI. The implementation and artifacts are assembled in the repository working tree; the final clean tagged build must pass Linux CI and add the immutable URL, release date, and version DOI. This document carries the full argument. The model results regenerate via scripts/run_baseline.py, run_part2.py, run_deep.py, and run_integrated.py; the canonical release manifest is outputs/MANIFEST.md, with an additional model-input manifest at outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md. The integrated-bootstrap layer reserves explicit terms for material flows, seed sizing, embodied autonomy, process-specific gravity, construction and commissioning, source transfers, a rate-limited Earth counterfactual, the intelligence–compute coupling, and debris state dynamics — and tests their consequences through declared, stylized proxies rather than resolving the underlying engineering. Every structural coefficient in that layer is ASSUMPTION-class; its outputs are scenario implications, not measurements, probabilities, engineering estimates, or forecasts. See Appendices B–D.

Abstract

This paper develops and tests a conditional thesis: advanced AI, reusable launch, robotics, energy systems, and automated manufacturing could be combined into an industrial system beyond Earth that maintains and expands its own productive capacity. This paper expands the object of analysis from an abstract industrial substrate to a capacity-expanding autonomous seed: physical equipment, embodied autonomy, software and simulation, industrial memory, experimental capacity, and material-category-resolved supply. Part I implements a ten-sector, multisector capacity model with decomposed depreciation, repair, recycling, stockpiles, imports, common-cause shocks, and architecture-specific constraints for LEO, the lunar surface, and Mars. Its unit-invariant replication metric is balanced capacity doubling; its endpoint is realized post-shock growth, and its bottleneck diagnostic is a finite 1% supply-response test with explicit co-binding. The assumption ensembles produce outcomes ranging from collapse to sustained expansion, with electronics dominant on the Moon, electronics and power on Mars, and captured/recovered feed dominant in LEO. The inherited model begins with positive capacity in all ten sectors and omits construction lags, commissioning, yield ramps, and minimum efficient scales; its doubling times are stylized capacity-model first passages, not factory-construction or seed-commissioning forecasts. Part II builds an affine levelized-cost model for terrestrial and space compute, separating integrated disposable satellites from serviceable/reusable platforms. After completing the system boundary with communications, ground network, spacecraft bus, program NRE, insurance, regulatory and disposal costs, residual value, thermal margins, and separate financing, generic LEO compute costs 5.29 times Earth on the serviceable-platform architecture and 6.74 times Earth if integrated and disposable; the disclosed Starmind AI1 mass case remains 3.17 and 3.80 times Earth, respectively. The analysis therefore supports neither a point forecast of autonomous industry nor present orbital-compute parity. It identifies the architecture-dependent measurements and demonstrations that would most change those conclusions. A new 18-sector, 17-material-group integrated-bootstrap model then represents an installed operating seed — physical equipment with stylized autonomy, intervention, construction, and commissioning constraints — and asks how much installed mass is sufficient, whether its material graph can close first on the Moon and later across asteroidal sources, and whether aggregate operating capacity can double without routine human intervention. Under the declared central assumptions, the minimum-mass lunar design retaining an Earth-supplied strategic-material import stock is 216.7 t installed — 58.1 t (27%) of it that stock — but its slowest normalized sector falls to 0.54 operating cell-equivalents by year 40; the configured strict lunar-only source graph is structurally infeasible, with the shortfall quantified per material category; and a synthetic composite Moon–asteroid portfolio satisfies the same seed-LP constraints at 185.5 t, crosses two at 34.75 years, and reaches 3.61 sector-balanced equivalents at year 40. Keeping all 18 sectors stateful changes the interpretation: the intelligence–industry coupling is nearly inert in the material-starved terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases but operative in the Moon–asteroid network, where removing it reduces year-40 balanced capacity from 3.61 to 2.70. The assumed AI level also binds statically through seed feasibility. These are deterministic consequences of a stipulated architecture and assumption ensemble (Part I.8), not seed designs, engineering estimates, or forecasts. The model operationalizes the coupled loop and sharpens its material and autonomy conditions; it does not demonstrate that the assumed processes, source portfolio, AI gains, or industrial closure exist.

Keywords: recursive industrial improvement; space manufacturing; industrial closure; orbital compute; lunar industry; multisector capacity; autonomous industrial seed; embodied autonomy; lunar materials; techno-economics; Monte Carlo.

Scope and Status

This is a strategic hypothesis and research program with, now, its first quantitative core — not a techno-economic demonstration. It identifies necessary conditions, bottlenecks, and discriminating tests for a self-expanding industrial system, computes what its own assumptions imply, and states throughout which of its six propositions each conclusion rests on.

The reference system in this paper is machine-only: no resident human population, agriculture, or biosphere-scale life-support loop is required for industrial reproduction. Human settlement can create demand and impose additional requirements, but it is not a prerequisite of the thesis. Water, hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen remain important as propellants, reductants, coolants, lubricants, polymers, process gases, and chemical feedstocks; removing agriculture narrows the closure problem but does not remove volatile chemistry from it.

Six distinct propositions run through this document and carry different evidence:

  • (P1) A recursively expanding industrial system is conceptually possible — a respectable case is made.
  • (P2) Such a system might eventually be technically feasible — quantitatively explored for both the inherited industrial substrate and a first explicit integrated bootstrap (Part I): outcomes span failure to sustained expansion across named assumption sets, with the feasibility margin localized to architecture-specific bottlenecks. The coupled intelligence–industry functions now have an operational stylized form, but their coefficients remain assumptions rather than evidence of complete-system feasibility (III.6).
  • (P3a) Orbital and lunar compute during the Earth-dependent bridge would be economically competitive — now quantified (Part II) and, at anchored values, negative, with crossover requiring a specific, currently unanchored corner of parameter space.
  • (P3b) A mature, high-closure space-industrial ecology would eventually obtain a structural economic advantage over terrestrial expansion — scenario-modeled but unresolved: a symmetric dynamic comparison now gives Earth and space the same investment, reinvestment, learning, depreciation, financing, regulatory-delay, demand, and resource mechanics, while space is capped by the physical trajectory and pays for industrial orders, transfer, and intervention. Neither commodity nor space-native cases become space-self-financing inside 40 years under the declared ASSUMPTION coefficients. This does not establish or refute mature real-world advantage.
  • (P4a) The companies are deliberately integrating launch, communications, AI, terrestrial and orbital compute, chip design and manufacture, and prospective off-world energy and manufacturing — documented as a declared portfolio direction, since SEC-filed offering materials associated with the S-1 (the Rule 433 free-writing prospectus and incorporated materials) name orbital compute, lunar manufacturing and energy, in-orbit manufacturing, manufacturing on the Moon and Mars, asteroid mining, and “interplanetary industrialization” among the initiatives (Form S-1 pp. 164, 171; roadshow slides 42–44) [S27]. Shared technical interfaces, binding cross-program milestones, and joint resource allocation are not publicly established.
  • (P4b) That this integration is intended to produce recursive industrial closure — inferential, with no closure program, seed bill of materials, reproduction metric, or minimum-cut roadmap published, and assessed against competing explanations (Part III).

The P4 split matters: the two halves carry materially different evidential status, and the earlier argument conflated them. Conclusions are licensed by the strongest proposition they rest on, not by the conjunction of all six.

Evidential classes. Documented statements; announced initiatives; technically grounded pathways; inferred strategy; speculative closure — as and adds one additional rung: computed, meaning derived mechanically from stated assumptions by the companion model (public repository with checksummed output manifest, Appendix C). A computed result inherits the epistemic class of its weakest input; structural coefficients are ASSUMPTION-class throughout, so no computed result is a measurement. Every computed number below carries its assumption-set label (conservative / central / optimistic); a result quoted without its set label is a misquotation.

Claim status and input provenance are separate taxonomies. The six evidential classes above qualify propositions and conclusions. Model inputs instead use five source classes: peer_reviewed, technical_report, reporting, company_statement, and ASSUMPTION. A computed output inherits the weakest input class in its dependency chain.

Executive Summary

This document develops a unified hypothesis: the deepest strategic value of advanced AI, reusable launch, energy systems, robotics, and automated manufacturing may lie in combining them into a recursively improving industrial system beyond Earth. The end state is not merely a rocket fleet, a settlement, a humanoid robot, or a frontier model, but a distributed industrial ecology able to sustain itself, expand productive capacity, and progressively reduce Earth dependence.

Central proposition. Once a space-based industrial system can obtain local energy and materials, maintain its machinery, manufacture additional productive equipment, and coordinate itself through AI, the primary constraint shifts from acquiring terrestrial inputs to allocating productive throughput over time.

That proposition distinguishes two growth regimes. An orbital data center whose servers, structures, power systems, and replacements continue to be made on Earth is deployed capacity, not a self-expanding industry:

dCorbitdt=qcLE→O(t)−δCCorbit. \frac{\mathrm d C_{\mathrm{orbit}}}{\mathrm d t} = q_c L_{E\rightarrow O}(t)-\delta_C C_{\mathrm{orbit}}.

At a constant Earth-to-orbit delivery rate LE→OL_{E\rightarrow O}, capacity grows approximately linearly while depreciation is small and ultimately approaches qcLE→O/δCq_cL_{E\rightarrow O}/\delta_C. By contrast, a closed industrial stock that allocates a fraction of its own output to producing additional productive equipment follows the idealized endogenous law

dHdt=(r−δH)H, \frac{\mathrm d H}{\mathrm d t}=(r-\delta_H)H,

and compounds only when r>δHr>\delta_H. Off-Earth location does not create that acceleration: reproductive closure does. The role of off-Earth industry is to combine that endogenous growth regime with access to matter, energy, and usable area outside Earth’s biosphere and society-priced siting constraints. Earth-fed orbital compute can therefore raise intelligence at a constant deployment rate without crossing the industrial-reproduction threshold; the two cases must not be conflated.

The framework contains two coupled loops. In the digital loop, AI improves software, research, engineering, evaluation, and coordination. In the physical loop, AI and robots improve mining, refining, power, manufacturing, construction, transport, and the production of additional compute. Each loop strengthens the other:

better intelligence → better automation → more productive capacity →
more compute → better intelligence

The economic argument compresses to two walls and two escapes. The capital wall: expansion purchased through markets runs into scarcity pricing and supply-elasticity limits as ambitions scale; the escape is self-replication, which re-denominates expansion from dollars into materials, energy, and time. The operating wall: on Earth, society-priced costs — land, permits, politics, waste heat — rise with scale and cannot be closed away; the escape is space, where permission attaches to the gateway rather than the complex. Both escapes pass through one passage: the bridge, in which the first self-replicating seed is bought at full market price, operated where depreciation is most severe, and financed by intermediate products.

This paper prices the passage and models the seed. Five headline results:

  1. The active bottleneck is architecture-specific. A unit-invariant finite-response diagnostic relaxes each material balance by 1%, then divides credit among rows whose positive response is within 5% of the largest. Electronics receives about 94–97% of co-binding credit on the lunar surface; electronics and power divide most credit on Mars; and capture/mining receives about 86–100% in LEO. The LEO architecture has no ore body and depends on captured and recovered feed. Import-cut experiments are small, margin-conditional samples, so their defensible executive-level result is ordinal rather than a precise frequency: import dependency is architecture-dependent, and electronics is often load-bearing where the sampled strategic-material gap is deepest. That identity is conditional on a homogeneous electronics-productivity assumption, not a measurement of real electronics closure.
  2. Balanced-capacity doubling and sustained expansion are different outcomes. The headline replication metric is λ(t) = min_j K_j(t)/K_j(0) ≥ 2: every modeled sector has doubled in its own capacity units. It is not a claim that a commissioned second physical factory exists. The endpoint records realized, post-shock growth; the pre-shock allocation endpoint remains a diagnostic. In the declared central sampling measure, expansion at year 30 occupies a much larger region than sustained positive realized growth throughout years 25–30. Median balanced doubling among sampled runs that reach it is about 26.0 years in LEO, 5.0 on the Moon, and 11.0 on Mars. Exact occupancy counts and intervals are reported in Part I.8. The Earth-import-cut LEO result is expressly conditional on continued capture feed and is not an autonomous-ecology result.
  3. The space-compute crossover is an architecture story, not a launch-price story. At central inputs, generic LEO compute is 5.29× Earth on a serviceable/reusable platform and 6.74× if the satellite is integrated and disposable. The Starmind AI1 disclosure scenario is 3.17× and 3.80×, respectively. No sampled point in the declared 2,000-draw shared design-space sweep favors space in any reported architecture/reference cell. This is design-space occupancy under the stated measure, not a calibrated probability. Negative median break-even launch prices show why: qualification cost, hardware and platform life, and utilization can dominate launch. The deterministic aspirational case is still 1.09× Earth after the completed cost boundary; the former incomplete-cost calculation was 0.76×. It combines company targets with three favorable, unpublished model bounds and is assigned no probability.
  4. The installed seed is a material-and-knowledge graph, not a cargo total. The new 18-sector, 17-material-group layer requires physical equipment, digital tools, industrial memory, experiments, task-resolved autonomy, gravity-compatible processes, and aggregate operating-capacity growth. The LP sizes an installed seed, while a separate deployment diagnostic moves delivered mass through staged, installed, commissioned, startup-failure, recovery, and operating states. For the lunar bridge, 216.7 t installed corresponds to 303.3 t delivered under the declared packaging, site, spares, calibration, and startup-energy assumptions. Its its doubling metric is first passage of the slowest normalized sector to two operating-cell equivalents, not a discretely commissioned second factory. Under the declared central assumptions, the lunar strategic-material bridge requires 216.7 t installed, of which 58.1 t (27%) is Earth-supplied strategic-material stock — a substantially Earth-provisioned seed, not a nearly closed one — but the slowest sector reaches only 0.54 cell-equivalents at year 40. The terrestrial rehearsal similarly reaches only 0.47. The configured strict lunar-only source graph is structurally infeasible — its trace inputs cannot supply the assumed electronics and process-equipment stack, in the central case and in every draw. A deliberately synthetic composite Moon–asteroid portfolio satisfies the same seed-LP constraints at 185.5 t, crosses two at 34.75 years, and reaches 3.61 sector-balanced equivalents at year 40. Across 200 deterministic assumption draws, the lunar-bridge, strict-lunar, and Moon–asteroid cases occupy the satisfying region in 126, 0, and 187 of 200 declared draws (the terrestrial rehearsal in 83). These counts describe design-space occupancy under the stated log-uniform measure, not empirical frequencies or success probabilities.
  5. The declared AI coupling matters only after material bottlenecks relax. In the terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases, material availability caps construction in roughly nine-tenths of quarterly steps, so coupling ablations change the year-40 endpoint by less than 0.1%. In the Moon–asteroid network, only 48/160 steps are material-limited and the fully uncoupled run reaches 2.70 balanced equivalents versus 3.61 at baseline — 65% of baseline net growth. This is a within-model regime change, not evidence that the stipulated AI coefficients are real. The assumed AI level is also load-bearing statically: at base autonomy the lunar-bridge and Moon–asteroid seeds fail the feasibility threshold outright. Only the Moon–asteroid network reaches two equivalents by year 40 and is terminal-window expanding.

The integrated layer also makes one architecture boundary stateful: industrial closure does not license a dense orbital shell. Active, derelict, and fragment stocks feed a five-year fragment creation-to-clearance ratio RdebrisR_{\mathrm{debris}} — a flow ratio over the final five years, not a branching-process reproduction number or a derived criticality threshold. In the declared year-40 scenarios, the Earth-fed orbital cases clear more fragments than they create (Rdebris=0.61R_{\mathrm{debris}}=0.61 with weak mitigation and 0.35 with strong), while dense endogenous deployment creates substantially more than it clears under both mitigation levels (R=4.79R=4.79 weak and 4.45 strong, while the fragment index falls from 3.84 to 2.21). This remains a stress-test indicator rather than a safety measure). A sparse distributed topology sits at the boundary ratio of 1.00 with an empty fragment stock only because its collision-kernel multiplier is explicitly set to 0.01. These are topology stress tests, not orbital traffic forecasts or cascade-threshold results [S45–S49].

The strategic assessment (Part III): the evidence documents an integrated off-world portfolio direction (P4a) but does not establish one coordinated technical architecture. The initiative list and first-party messaging rule out a purely terrestrial reading, while the matched H0 still explains co-ownership, portfolio promotion, supply hedging, and adjacent commercial projects without a common systems plan. It does not establish recursive closure as the objective (P4b): the closure-specific observables — seed bills of materials, reproduction metrics, minimum-cut roadmaps, locally reproducible production equipment — remain absent. What has changed is that the discriminating indicators are now model-ranked: the rational next moves of a closure-seeking actor — electronics-closure engineering, loss-tolerant orbital-compute persistence, materials-recovery recycling — are exactly the observations the models identify as informative.

How to read this document

The four parts carry different kinds of claim and can be read independently:

  • Part I is model: the inherited ten-sector capacity model and the new integrated-bootstrap layer. Its results are computed implications of declared assumption sets, never measurements. The canonical numeric tables are in I.8; every restatement elsewhere (Abstract, this summary, III.6, IV.1) follows them.
  • Part II is techno-economics: the levelized-cost crossover model and its reconciliation with independent studies. Canonical tables in II.3.
  • Part III is interpretation: an ordinal, evidence-tabled assessment of corporate strategy. It contains no model outputs, only their use as ranking criteria for observables.
  • Part IV is quarantined scenario extrapolation plus the limitations statement; nothing in it feeds back into Parts I–II.

Readers who want only the load-bearing results should read the Executive Summary, I.8, II.3, and the Limitations section. The epistemic rules — source classes, ASSUMPTION labeling, and the frequency-not-probability convention — are defined in Scope and Status and apply everywhere. Appendix A carries parameter provenance, Appendix B the revision history (including what changed under each external review), Appendix C reproducibility, and Appendix D the complete model specification.

Part I — Technical Feasibility

I.1 Recursive self-improvement: the digital loop

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) occurs when an intelligent system contributes to the process that produces a more capable successor. The useful unit is not a public model release but a verified improvement loop: identify a weakness, propose a change, run an experiment, evaluate, deploy, and use the improved system to accelerate the next cycle.

I(t+1)=I(t)+ΔI(t),ΔI=L×G \begin{aligned} I(t+1) &= I(t) + \Delta I(t), \\ \Delta I &= L \times G \end{aligned}

I is effective intelligence; L is the number of useful loops completed; G is the average gain per successful loop. The loop rate is constrained by the least scalable part of the development system:

L=min⁡{LC(C),LD(D),LX(X),LV(V),LR(R)} L = \min\!\left\{L_C(C), L_D(D), L_X(X), L_V(V), L_R(R)\right\}

— each conversion function turning its resource (compute, data, experimental throughput, verification capacity, deployment reliability) into verified loops per unit time. Efficiency is partly a function of intelligence, E(t) = f(I(t)): more capable systems may improve coding, architecture search, synthetic-data generation, hardware design, factory scheduling, scientific modeling, and evaluation design. The form of f — logarithmic, linear, superlinear, saturating — is unknown; a rigorous analysis identifies which regime observed loop completion supports rather than assuming takeoff. Public releases are lagging indicators; the strategically relevant measure is verified improvement loops per calendar time. The verification term V recurs in a second role as the governing safety constraint (Part III.4). Time-spaced releases nevertheless remain useful: they generate real-world feedback, revenue, reliability data, and operational learning. A release is part of the loop, but it is not the loop.

I.2 Recursive industrial improvement: the physical loop

Digital intelligence depends on a physical substrate: chips, data centers, electricity, cooling, networks, factories, labor, materials, logistics, maintenance — a dependency inventory, not a sum; any term can bind. The physical recursive loop begins when AI and robotics improve the production of those inputs: better intelligence designs and operates better machines; better machines expand energy and manufacturing; expanded industry produces more compute; more compute supports better intelligence.

Energy hardware is not energy: “with solar, energy equals hardware” expresses a recursion, not an identity. Installed arrays generate power that supports production of additional arrays; the system still pays in materials, machine-hours, maintenance, and conversion losses. Robotic labor is manufactured productive capacity: when robots participate in producing factories, energy systems, and additional robots, labor becomes partially reproducible, and the robot reproduction ratio must exceed one after depreciation, failures, and the equipment needed for high-complexity components — stated with the horizon and unit it requires, R_robot,T = discounted lifetime robot-equivalent capacity produced over T ÷ robot-equivalent capacity retired, consumed, or irreversibly committed over T, since a factory is not “consumed” merely because it helped build robots. In the long run the decisive competitive variable — under the threshold-like, small-α branch of the capability model examined in II.5 — is not model quality but the doubling time of productive hardware — and Part I.4 examines what that replication must outrun.

The embodied-autonomy threshold. A mobile manipulator can have enough joints, reach, payload, sensing, and tool interfaces to span many industrial tasks without being able to close the labor loop. Kinematic sufficiency is not cognitive sufficiency. The threshold relevant here is whether the combined robot-and-AI system can diagnose unfamiliar faults, choose and use tools, execute long-horizon construction and repair, recover from failed actions, learn from intervention, and verify that the restored machine is safe to return to service. Present humanoid programs, including Optimus, are evidence of an intended general-purpose hardware form, not evidence that this unscripted industrial task set has been solved. The paper therefore treats embodied autonomy as task coverage and recovery capability, not as robot count or degrees of freedom.

The loops couple through a second channel: data as the exhaust of the physical loop. Operating physical industry generates data that exists nowhere else — test telemetry, process parameters, failure archives, fleet traces. It commoditizes less readily than public text, for four reasons: negative results (the map of what does not work survives only in the archives of whoever paid for the failures); sim-to-real ground truth (real telemetry is the verification fuel for AI-proposed physical designs); legal fencing (export-controlled data cannot lawfully enter open corpora — and equally cannot feed publicly served models, so the strongest-moat data is harvestable only in an internal, access-controlled variant); and temporal lead time (longitudinal data imposes a minimum calendar-time barrier to a like-for-like archive: a rival beginning today matches the sampling rate but cannot reproduce the historical intervention-and-outcome sequence retroactively, though capital compresses much of the disadvantage through acquisition, larger current fleets, accelerated and parallel experimentation, simulation, transfer learning, and newer processes that make the old archive less relevant [S34] — a lead-time barrier, not an impossibility). The data-closure index κ_D is a direction-of-effort indicator, not a computable ratio: its denominator is not measurable, and value depends on quality, linkage, and integration, not origin. The honest caveat: proprietary physical data is lead time, not permanence — any actor operating comparable fleets and factories generates comparable exhaust, at national scale in China’s case.

The public record supplies two applications of the same supplemental-training mechanism, which is evidence of an emerging pattern rather than proof of a repeatable one. In July 2026, days after an in-house engineering model was reported to have received a supplemental pass over the coding data of an acquired developer-tools company, Musk said that the SpaceX engineering corpus — excluding ITAR-controlled material — would enter supplemental training of its roughly two-trillion-parameter successor [S11–S13]. The relevant advantage is therefore not raw ownership alone:

D_advantage = f(uniqueness, causal linkage, coverage, quality,
                accessibility, integration, verification value)

Generation is insufficient; the data must be integrated and attributable enough to train on. Tesla’s first CIO has described building the custom Warp enterprise system in roughly four months in 2012 after the company rejected off-the-shelf ERP, then extending it continuously so operations could change without waiting on a vendor [S15]. SpaceX independently built its own internal manufacturing and enterprise system, Warp Drive [S16]. The convergence on the same build-don’t-buy pattern is evidence that iteration speed, not a common brand name, drives the architecture.

Commentary describes the resulting ideal as a unified build record for each produced unit: as designed (models and simulations), as built (supplier batches, process settings, torques, and factory tests), and as deployed (fleet telemetry). Integrated cross-functional data and over-the-air learning are independently documented; the exact tri-phase schema is only partially confirmed and is treated as indicative [S14–S17]. Its analytical importance is the causal linkage from design intent through production parameters to field behavior — the quality dimension of κ_D.

For an autonomous seed, this record is more than training data: it is part of the transported productive system. Process recipes, material models, calibration procedures, controller firmware, CAD/CAM files, compilers, simulators, verification suites, dependency mirrors, failure histories, and intervention records determine whether physical equipment can be operated, repaired, and adapted after communication or supply is cut. The manuscript calls this package industrial memory. It is not equivalent to “all industrial knowledge,” an incoherent completion standard; it is a machine-readable operating foundation coupled to the experimental capacity to discover what the initial package omitted.

Scale proxies require disciplined interpretation. By mid-2026 the vehicle fleet had accumulated more than ten billion miles under supervised autonomy, against roughly 220 million fully driverless miles disclosed by another operator [S17, S30]. No valid conversion exists between those regimes, so the figures are not an advantage multiple. More informative disclosures concern structure: an occupancy network trained on 1.4 billion fleet video frames and an auto-labeling system replacing roughly five million hours of manual annotation [S17]. The aerospace analogue is thirteen heavy-lift flight tests by mid-2026: few observations, each with high information content [S31]. These quantities demonstrate data generation and integration capacity, not autonomous industrial closure.

I.3 Why space changes the cost structure

On Earth, useful locations compete with communities, ecosystems, jurisdictions, and alternative uses. Off Earth, the monetary price of unused area approaches zero — but infrastructure does not become free; the cost changes kind, from purchasing scarce terrestrial sites and coordinating human institutions toward transporting, converting, and maintaining matter through an automated production network:

Earth: land + permits + construction + energy + materials + labor + coordination
Space: transport + energy + extraction + refining + manufacturing + maintenance + coordination

The land term declines sharply, but useful positions can remain scarce because of illumination, thermal conditions, communications geometry, orbital stability, resource proximity, political accessibility, and transport energy. The first system must still arrive, survive, obtain or import matter, reject heat, maintain operations, and replace failed equipment. Space removes neither scarcity nor cost; it changes their composition.

The standard external objections — station-keeping, collision management, imported mass, maintenance, coordination — become internal product categories once the complex can manufacture the required systems: propellant lines, tracking and maneuver capability, local extraction and recycling, inspection robots and modular spares, compute and communications. The crucial question is never whether these requirements exist but whether the complex can reproduce the industries that satisfy them faster than the system depreciates.

This is the causal boundary of the expansion claim. Moving an Earth-manufactured factory or data center into orbit changes its environmental and transport terms but leaves its growth exogenous to the off-world system. Moving a reproducible production graph off Earth does two different things: closure makes growth endogenous, while location relaxes terrestrial biosphere, land, and political rate limits. Either property can exist without the other. “Free industrial expansion” is shorthand for their conjunction, never for costless matter, energy, control, or time.

Gravity is a process variable, not a system prerequisite. Industrial operations divide into at least three classes: processes that tolerate or benefit from microgravity; bulk operations for which a stable downward acceleration assists excavation, hopper flow, phase separation, drainage, and conventional machine layout; and processes that need a specified acceleration, hydrostatic head, or convection regime. Lunar gravity (approximately 0.165g0.165g) supplies the second class with a persistent “down,” although lower weight also reduces traction and changes granular flow. It cannot be declared sufficient for every casting, chemical, lubrication, thermal, or separation process without testing that process.

Where greater acceleration is needed, the relevant intervention is normally a rotating drum, centrifuge, or production module—not artificial gravity for the entire industrial ecology. For radius RR and angular speed ω\omega,

ac=ω2R. a_c=\omega^2R.

One terrestrial gg requires about 30 rpm at a one-meter radius or 9.5 rpm at ten meters. An ideal rotor consumes energy to spin up and stores E=12Iω2E=\tfrac12 I\omega^2; it does not require continuous power merely to remain in uniform rotation. The engineering cost lies in structural mass, containment, bearings or magnetic suspension, balance control, vibration, rotating power/data interfaces, spin losses, maintenance, and the inability to share one acceleration geometry across every process. Lunar gravity is therefore plausibly enough for many bulk operations, while local centrifugation is the fallback for gravity-sensitive steps. No credible single dollar estimate exists without a process list, throughput, rotor radius, and maintenance architecture. The inherited ten-sector model has none of these variables; the integrated layer adds declared per-process gravity requirements, centrifuge radii, and structural-mass and parasitic-power penalties (D.1) — stylized equipment overheads, not simulations of the underlying processes.

The complex need not be one self-contained factory: a distributed network of specialized nodes — lunar mines, orbital refineries, propellant depots, solar arrays, shipyards, robot factories, compute centers — whose combined input-output graph is closed. A caution on aggregation applies to every use of the word “space” in this document: LEO, high orbit, cislunar space, the lunar poles, Mars, and asteroids differ in radiation, thermal cycling, illumination, dust, gravity, resources, transport energy, and serviceability. Feasibility claims cannot be aggregated across them; the model of Part I.7 therefore uses three explicit reference architectures (LEO / lunar surface / Mars) rather than “space.”

I.4 Depreciation: the harsh term

dHdt=(r−δ)H \frac{\mathrm d H}{\mathrm d t} = (r-\delta)H

Every claim ultimately reduces to whether gross replication r exceeds depreciation δ. Terrestrial industry operates inside an ambient repair economy; space assets have none of it.

Published measurements constrain a few component classes without bounding the depreciation of an autonomous industrial ecology:

  • GEO solar arrays degrade 0.4–1.7%/yr [S19], overlapping a terrestrial PV median of 0.5–0.6%/yr at the low end and reaching several times it at the high end [S18] — one component class, silent about bearings, seals, lubricated mechanisms, batteries, machine tools, robots, radiators, dust-exposed joints, and optical metrology.
  • Constellation figures are cohort-dependent: reported early-generation failure fractions near 3% fall below 0.5% for later generations, the underlying tracker separates early deorbit, uncontrolled decay, retirement, and disposal, and a fleet fraction without a cohort definition, observation interval, and satellite-years is not a hazard rate [S22].
  • Large-training-run figures near one interruption per two thousand accelerator-days mix permanent component failures with recoverable host, network, and software events, most automatically recovered: a cluster interruption frequency, not a component hazard rate.

The space penalty is not faster wear — it is the five-to-fifteen-year no-repair design envelope, the internality of every repair chain, and discrete loss without salvage. Meanwhile the most advanced terrestrial capital — fab tools on 2–5-year schedules, accelerators retired within 3–6 years — is written off faster than a space solar array physically degrades, because obsolescence sets the terrestrial clock.

Five quantities must be kept apart: physical degradation, functional failure, accounting depreciation, economic obsolescence, and frontier-equivalent capacity loss. The last two are not physical — an accelerator does not vanish because a better one exists — so obsolescence enters a growth equation only where H is measured in quality-adjusted or frontier-equivalent capacity, which is why the terrestrial paradox above is a statement about accounting and frontier equivalence rather than about matter. The corrected form, decomposed per environment,

δtotal=δwear+δcatastrophic+δobsolescence+δlogistics \delta_{\mathrm{total}} = \delta_{\mathrm{wear}} + \delta_{\mathrm{catastrophic}} + \delta_{\mathrm{obsolescence}} + \delta_{\mathrm{logistics}}

is what the model implements per sector and per location: space raises the catastrophic and logistics terms, Earth raises the obsolescence term, wear differs modestly. The environment drives δ upward through radiation, thermal cycling, micrometeoroids and debris, vacuum effects, regolith dust, and the absence of an ambient repair economy.

Collision-cascade boundary. Kessler risk is not an unusually large independent shock. It is positive feedback: collisions create orbiting fragments, those fragments raise the later collision rate, and a sufficiently dense region can keep generating debris after new deployment stops [S45]. The implemented LEO debris_event instead has a fixed 0.05 yr⁻¹ Poisson rate and removes a sampled 0.02–0.10 fraction from selected sectors; the loss creates no debris and the event rate does not depend on deployed capacity. The continuous catastrophic term is likewise an exogenous hazard range. These terms can represent ordinary impact exposure but cannot test the cascade threshold, avoidance saturation, shell-to-shell fragment transport, or recovery through decay and active removal. Accordingly, every LEO scale result in I.8 is conditional on a debris regime in which fragment creation does not outrun clearance. The missing state is not assigned a silent proxy value. The integrated layer supplies both an aggregate stress test and a second, finite-mass diagnostic resolving 400-km LEO, 650-km LEO, and cislunar regions; active assets, intact derelicts, trackable and untrackable fragments; collision-generated yield; avoidance saturation; cross-shell transport; disposal, natural clearance, retrieval, and active removal. It reports expected hazardous descendants per object as a branching-style stress metric (I.8, D.1). The kernels and transitions remain assumptions rather than a conjunction-assessment or validated traffic model. Lunar orbit does not remove the issue: breakup simulations find strongly orbit-dependent evolution, including long-lasting debris in some low lunar orbits and nonuniform lunar impact patterns [S46].

One environment-specific case partly cuts the other way, and it is narrower than earlier drafts of this argument claimed. For short-lived compute payloads in very low orbit, aligning useful life with accelerator-obsolescence cycles reduces the economic value of repair: hardware retired within a few years regardless costs less to be unable to fix. The qualifications are substantial. Natural decay depends on altitude, ballistic coefficient, and solar activity — small spacecraft near 400 km can decay within five years, but beyond 500 km five-year decay is not assured and some objects persist for decades. The leading published orbital-compute architecture in fact places its cluster near 650 km in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit, chosen for illumination rather than disposal [S32], so the concession does not describe that design. Nor is disposal free: station-keeping, collision avoidance (SpaceX reports more than 1,000 automated Starlink avoidance manoeuvres per day in 2025, Form S-1 pp. 9 and 153 [S27]), replacement launch, network spares, and residual capital loss all remain — and the same source that calls orbital repair impracticable proposes redundant provisioning instead, which is a cost, not its absence [S32]. The concession therefore covers some payload classes in very low orbit and does not generalize: mines, refineries, machine tools, and robots must last decades to close a loop. In these models it lands in Part II (compute payloads), while Part I’s industrial δ decomposition stands.

The clock-setting component. In any partially closed system, the component with the shortest replacement horizon that cannot yet be produced or stockpiled locally sets a hard clock on the entire complex. Closure priority follows failure rate × non-replaceability, not mass fraction. Viability requires:

Treplenish,j<Teffectivesurvival,jfor every critical component class j T_{\mathrm{replenish},j} < T_{\mathrm{effective\ survival},j} \qquad \text{for every critical component class } j

Effective survival includes installed redundancy, spare inventory, repair probability, and substitution — not time to first failure; the naive form ignored inventories, cannibalisation, and stockpiling, all of which the model carries explicitly. Part I.7 enforces the condition by construction, and Part I.8 identifies the clock-setting sector by computation.

I.5 Industrial closure: the decisive threshold

Self-sustaining (P ≥ D: replacing what is consumed and lost) and self-expanding (P > D: net additional capacity) are different milestones.

gH=P−DH g_H = \frac{P-D}{H}

P is productive capacity manufactured during the period, D is capacity lost or consumed, and g_H is the net growth rate of productive infrastructure H. Industrial closure measures how much of the critical input set is produced inside the network:

κ=critical inputs produced internallytotal critical inputs required \kappa = \frac{\text{critical inputs produced internally}} {\text{total critical inputs required}}

At low closure, nearly all equipment arrives from Earth. At intermediate closure, local industry supplies propellant, shielding, structural material, tanks, roads, landing pads, and simple machines. At high closure, the network also supplies motors, sensors, precision tools, computers, robots, spacecraft, factory machinery, high-purity chemicals, and semiconductor equipment. The progression is descriptive, not a scalar score: the identity and replaceability of the residual imports determine whether the system is actually autonomous.

The scalar form is vocabulary, not measure: a system supplying 99.9% of its mass locally has effectively zero autonomous closure if the residual 0.1% contains irreplaceable electronics. The proper object is a vector — κ = (κ_power, κ_mining, κ_refining, κ_robotics, κ_machine-tools, κ_electronics, κ_thermal, κ_transport) — with minimum cut sets: the smallest combinations of imported inputs whose loss collapses the network. The clock-setting component is the scalar shadow of this vector structure. The hardest closure problem is the deep technological stack — precision metrology, advanced electronics, semiconductor fabrication, optics, high-purity processing, specialized alloys, software verification, and the machines that make those machines (Part III.2 examines the first announced attempt on its terrestrial face).

Lineage. The 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study [S23] designed a proof-of-principle self-replicating lunar factory growing from a ~100-ton seed and introduced quantitative closure analysis; Freitas and Merkle catalogued the design space [S24]. The present thesis is that lineage plus three ingredients the 1980 study lacked: general-purpose AI for coordination and redesign; a reusable heavy-lift transport economy; mass-manufactured robotics.

The r and κ anchors, read honestly. Three quantities sometimes presented as converging near one year are not commensurable: solar energy payback (0.9–4.1 yr [S20]) measures energy self-financing only; the NASA ~1-year figure is a strawman replication target adopted for a proof-of-principle design, with component values its authors described as crude estimates; Gigafactory Shanghai’s ten months is project execution inside a mature host economy. The replication time of a full industrial ecosystem is unknown — and here it appears only as a computed output distribution (Part I.8). For κ, the honest headline is a theory-versus-demonstration gap, stated as its authors did: the 90–96% figure is closure reported in earlier studies of specific nonreplicating space-production applications, cited in support of plausibility arguments, and the 1980 study explicitly placed a rigorous demonstration that its factory could produce every required part beyond its own scope [S23]. Against that sit gram-per-hour oxygen and ~20% single-output yields actually demonstrated [S21]; full-system closure has not been demonstrated at any scale. Stating the gap converts the indicators of Part III.5 from rhetoric into measurable distance.

The seed-factory transition. Earth stops transporting finished infrastructure and transports a compact industrial seed, but “seed” denotes four inseparable layers:

  1. Physical seed: power, extraction, refining, manufacturing, robots, compute, repair capability, laboratories, and initial spares.
  2. Digital seed: AI weights, firmware, controllers, compilers, CAD/CAM, simulators, optimization and verification tools, and locally available software dependencies.
  3. Industrial memory: process recipes, material and equipment models, calibration and maintenance procedures, complete build records, failure histories, intervention traces, and provenance.
  4. Experimental capacity: instrumentation, metrology, test stands, flexible machine tools, and the ability to run controlled experiments that produce missing knowledge.

The package is viable only if it grows its productive base before critical imported components fail. A credible design requires redundancy, recycling, buffers, and an explicit path for every nonlocal dependency. No finite seed can encode “all necessary industrial knowledge”; the operational criterion is a sufficient foundation plus the capacity to diagnose gaps, run experiments, validate new processes, and incorporate the results into industrial memory. The inherited ten-sector model represents only part of the physical layer: spares are a shelf-life-limited stockpile state; nonlocal dependencies are import lines that can be cut; and the “explicit path” is an abstract sector requirement matrix. The integrated layer sizes the seed and adds stylized representations of the remaining layers — a fixed 5 t digital-seed mass, task-coverage autonomy, intervention budgets, and commissioning dynamics (I.7, D.1). Those are declared proxies, not resolved requirements: collapsing storage, compute, calibration standards, laboratory machinery, consumables, and test articles into one constant means the model cannot yet determine which component of knowledge closure binds.

I.6 Intelligence, coordination, and time

A sufficiently capable AI converts much of organizational coordination from human management into a computational service: scheduling machines, allocating energy, routing materials, diagnosing failures, redesigning components, balancing inventories, planning construction, and selecting the next bottleneck to expand.

Coordination burden = f(number of agents, complexity, uncertainty,
                        intelligence)

As intelligence and local autonomy improve, human management per unit of infrastructure can decline. The likely architecture is hierarchical rather than perfectly centralized: local controllers manage fast operations; facility-level agents coordinate production; higher-level planners allocate resources across the network.

An early terrestrial version is documented inside the same corporate ecosystem, though more weakly than some commentary claims. The confirmed systems provide real-time monitoring, production scheduling, quality management, and linked operational data at factory scale [S14–S17]. That is evidence that coordination functions traditionally mediated by human management are already becoming industrial data infrastructure. Claims that the systems replace management wholesale remain commentary-class and are not used here.

Coordination cannot reach zero. Machines must sense their environment; signals require propagation time; fabrication and motion take time; uncertain results require verification; and two projects cannot consume the same indivisible machine or stored resource simultaneously:

Cmin=Csensing+Clatency+Cverification+Ccontention C_{\min} = C_{\mathrm{sensing}} + C_{\mathrm{latency}} + C_{\mathrm{verification}} + C_{\mathrm{contention}}

The strongest claim is therefore that coordination approaches a physical information floor, not zero. Intelligence compresses planning and management overhead until observation, propagation, actuation, and verification dominate.

After high closure the central allocation question changes from “can the system obtain land, permits, workers, components?” to “how much productive throughput should be assigned, and when will output be complete?”

Hcreated(t)=∫0tthroughput⁡(τ)dτ H_{\mathrm{created}}(t) = \int_0^t \operatorname{throughput}(\tau)\,\mathrm d\tau

Scarcity becomes latency: outputs remain scarce because machines, energy, compute, transport capacity, and time have alternative uses, but the accounting unit shifts toward joules, kilograms processed, machine-hours, compute-hours, delta-v, and completion time. In the mature regime, growth is bottleneck-limited:

dHdt=(r(I,E,M)−δ)H \frac{\mathrm d H}{\mathrm d t} = \bigl(r(I,E,M)-\delta\bigr)H

When r exceeds δ, the idealized solution is exponential growth; real systems instead move through phases in which extraction, refining, power, thermal control, transport, precision manufacturing, compute, or maintenance is slowest. Intelligence accelerates growth by detecting and expanding that active bottleneck. The model below is an idealized, perfectly informed coordination benchmark, not a demonstration that an AI can observe, verify, and execute the allocation across a distributed factory. Within that benchmark, the co-binding set reported each step identifies the modeled active bottleneck.

I.7 The multisector model

The model that produces a real number needs, per critical sector, a capacity, a sector-specific depreciation, a requirement matrix, and import terms — with self-expansion defined as feasible positive net growth in every indispensable sector. The framework specifies it and the repository builds and runs it [S28]. Its elements:

  • Ten sectors: power, mining, refining, robotics, machine tools, electronics, thermal, transport, and — as first-class service sectors — repair and recycling. Repair offsets the wear component of δ only, at an efficiency cost and a spares bill drawn from the requirement matrix; recycling converts retiring capacity into secondary mining/refining feed, capped by the scrap flow.
  • Requirement matrix A[i,j]: units of sector-i output consumed to build one unit of sector-j capacity. ASSUMPTION-class, existing only inside named assumption sets (conservative / central / optimistic).
  • Decomposed δ per environment (I.4’s four components, per sector), assembled from anchored ranges where anchors exist and declared ASSUMPTION entries elsewhere. Retirement does not become fully recyclable scrap: environment- and loss-specific recovery factors distinguish wear, catastrophic loss, obsolescence, and logistics loss, and repaired wear is subtracted from retirement. Each resolved value carries a provenance record into the generated reports.
  • The allocation step: a three-stage lexicographic optimization. Stage 1 maximizes worst-case sector growth g over builds, wear repair, recycling, and stockpile drawdown. Stage 2 holds g at its optimum and minimizes normalized stock draw. Stage 3 holds both objectives and solves a strictly convex, normalized quadratic program over actions. This final tie-breaker makes the state transition unique instead of accepting an arbitrary LP vertex.
  • Strategic imported-part stockpiles with shelf life (electronics-class parts decay in storage), per-sector import cutoffs, Mars synodic pulse deliveries, and Poisson common-cause shocks hitting correlated sector groups (dust storms, solar storms, common design faults).
  • Three reference architectures: LEO (no ore body — feed imported or recycled from on-orbit mass), lunar surface (regolith feed, abrasive dust, no magnetosphere), Mars (deepest logistics penalty, ~26-month synodic resupply pulses, dust storms).

The electronics strategic-material gap. One structural parameter dominates the scoped scalar-anchor screen in I.8: the fraction of the electronics sector’s output mix producible off-world (sampled 0.10–0.30; ASSUMPTION with a documented bounding argument — advanced-node logic and memory are not locally closable in this scenario class; boards, passives, and power electronics plausibly are). No published measurement exists. Among the quantities currently parameterized, anchoring it is the highest-value observation this program could acquire; that ranking does not cover omitted structural uncertainties.

Integrated-bootstrap layer. The inherited model asks whether ten abstract capacities can grow together. The new model asks whether a declared physical seed can supply the material, service, autonomy, and commissioning requirements of another operating cell. It expands the graph to 18 sectors — separating interconnects/boards, passives/power, sensors/control, packaging/test, mature logic, advanced logic/memory, and process equipment/metrology — and 17 material categories (15 elements plus rare-earth and dopant classes; the model is material-category-resolved, not element-resolved — stoichiometric and process-chemical closure is not checked at the species level). Its material balance is

ΔMe=∑sYs,eXs+Ie+∑aFa,ein−∑jBe,jxj−Le−∑aFa,eout, \Delta M_e = \sum_s Y_{s,e}X_s + I_e + \sum_a F^{\mathrm{in}}_{a,e} - \sum_j B_{e,j}x_j - L_e - \sum_a F^{\mathrm{out}}_{a,e},

with explicit Earth→Moon strategic-material stock, asteroid→Moon feed, and Moon→orbit finished-compute arcs. The seed optimizer includes task coverage and residual intervention, construction lags, yield ramps, minimum viable scale, and process-specific gravity or centrifuge overhead. A dynamic pass then requires constructed capacity to ramp through commissioning before it contributes to the operating cell-equivalent aggregate. The equations, scenario definitions, and reproducibility record are in Appendix D and outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md.

I.8 Results

Monte Carlo over anchored ranges with common-cause shocks (n = 400 sampled runs per cell; one shared draw per anchor per run, correlating parameter uncertainty across sectors; every replication time is an output). The state metrics are:

  • Balanced doubling (headline replication metric). λ(t) = min_j K_j(t)/K_j(0); balanced doubling occurs when λ ≥ 2 — every modeled sector has at least doubled in its own capacity units. This is a balanced-capacity event, not a claim that a complete commissioned second plant or physical seed exists. λ is invariant to each sector’s arbitrary capacity unit, which the previous metric was not.
  • Aggregate doubling (continuity only). First passage of Σ_j K_j to 2× its initial value. This depends on the arbitrary units the sectors are denominated in and can be reached by overbuilding easy sectors while a hard sector lags; this aggregate metric is retained only for continuity.
  • Endpoint hierarchy. Reported timestamps are step ends. (1) expanding@30 — realized post-shock worst-sector state change g > 0 at year 30, the weakest endpoint: such a run may still be import- and stock-supported; (2) pre-shock allocation endpoint — the optimizer’s intended g before shocks, retained as a diagnostic rather than the headline; (3) sustained — realized g > 0 at every step ending in years 25–30; (4) Earth-import cutoff — a separate central-set ensemble with all Earth imports cut at year 30, counting runs with realized g > 0 throughout 30–35 (stock draw permitted). In LEO, captured feed continues, so that row is labeled Earth import cutoff with continued capture feed, not autonomy. None of these frequencies is called a real-world probability.
  • Binding sector and co-binding. Each material-balance supply is relaxed by 1%, the allocation is re-solved, and the finite improvement in worst-case growth is measured. The perturbation is relative and therefore invariant to row units. Rows within 5% of the largest positive response form a co-binding set and share fractional credit. This replaces both the unit-sensitive slack heuristic and the degenerate LP-dual label.

The machine-readable outputs report two doubling denominators because they answer different questions: ever doubled is the first-passage time among all runs that ever reach the criterion within 35 yr (transient growth capacity); survivor-conditioned restricts to runs also expanding at year 30 (sustained expansion performance). The visible table below displays the ever-doubled denominator; survivor-conditioned counts and times remain in the CSV. The difference is a distinct outcome class — runs that doubled early and then lost viability. All shares are frequencies across this stipulated assumption ensemble and shock process — not empirical probabilities of real-world success (machine-readable table: outputs/tables/mc_deep.csv):

Inherited-model boundary. Every run starts with positive capacity in all ten sectors. This layer has no construction lag, commissioning, yield ramp, or minimum efficient plant scale, and it permits continuous fractional capacity. Its reported years are stylized first-passage times inside an already complete abstract seed, not engineering schedules for a transported factory. The separate integrated layer below adds a physical seed and commissioning dynamics, but remains assumption-class.

All doubling columns below are balanced capacity events (λ ≥ 2: every modeled sector doubled in its own units); the aggregate-metric columns live in the CSV. LEO rows describe the import/capture-supported orbital recycling network of I.6, not an autonomous ecology.
