Earth-import cutoff (central set, all Earth imports cut at year 30; endpoint = realized g > 0 at each step ending in the 30–35 window):

env / qualification positive realized growth at year 35 after Earth-import cutoff, stock draw permitted (share, 95% CI) sustained positive realized growth throughout years 30–35 pre-shock allocation endpoint
LEO — Earth import cutoff with continued capture feed 210/400 (0.53, 0.48–0.57) 88 224
lunar 170/400 (0.42, 0.38–0.47) 23 187
Mars 53/400 (0.13, 0.10–0.17) 2 64

Reading: the conservative ensemble mostly fails on the realized endpoint: 3% of LEO, 8% of lunar, and 0.5% (2/400) of Mars runs are expanding at year 30. Central results are architecture-dependent: the realized endpoint is 67% in LEO, 56% on the Moon, and 15% on Mars, while only 31%, 5%, and 1% of all runs, respectively, remain positive throughout years 25–30. The gap between the pre-shock allocation endpoint and the realized endpoint is the cost of shocks at the reported step. The Mars synodic pulse can still flatter a single endpoint; λ = 0.55 and 4/400 sustained central runs show that contraction is the more informative reading there.

Balanced doubling is faster on the Moon but the endpoint is more sustained in LEO: among runs that ever reach λ ≥ 2, the central median is 5.0 years on the Moon versus 26.0 in LEO. These are balanced-capacity first passages, not construction records for complete second factories. LEO has no ore body, so growth is throttled by captured and recovered material. Recycling yield is below unity and recovery now depends on loss type; recycling alone cannot fund net expansion. The LEO Earth-import-cut row therefore preserves capture feed and must not be described as autonomy. The lunar surface has regolith feed and can grow quickly when electronics permits, while the finite-response diagnostic assigns about 96% of central lunar co-binding credit to electronics. The spread is the result: current evidence does not close feasibility, but the model identifies the conditional measurements that would.

Cut sets and the ensemble-frequent minimum cut. At central anchor values no import cut set is fatal by year 30 anywhere — imports accelerate but are not load-bearing at central values. That statement misleads alone, because cuts appear near the feasibility margin. Over sampled anchors (n = 40 draws per cell), conditional on an otherwise-expanding draw, central lunar electronics and the all-import cut coincide in this regeneration; central LEO is more exposed to the feed loop as a whole than to electronics alone; and the small central Mars survivor set produces no fatal candidate cut in this regeneration. Exact conditional frequencies have moved materially across equally valid small-n regenerations. They are reported in outputs/report_deep.md for reproducibility, but the defensible claim is ordinal: cut dependence appears near the feasibility margin and is architecture-specific; this experiment does not estimate a stable real-world probability. Capacity knockouts at central values: the eight physical production sectors (power, mining, refining, robotics, machine tools, electronics, thermal, transport) are knockout-indispensable in both architectures tested; repair is additionally indispensable on the lunar surface. With LEO’s 5% capture feed, a recycling knockout is survivable at central values. The structural point is: the LEO architecture lives on recovered and captured mass (capture/mining receives 98% of central co-binding credit), so its dependency is the feed loop as a whole rather than any single import line.

The clock-setting curve. Expansion frequency against the e-folding time of Earth-supply withdrawal (n = 60 per grid point; machine-readable: outputs/tables/import_decay_deep.csv): on the lunar surface under central assumptions, the realized year-30 endpoint is 0.40, 0.57, 0.43, 0.57, and 0.73 at 4-, 7-, 10-, 15-, and 25-year e-folding times. The non-monotonic wobble is within binomial noise at this n. The experiment is suggestive of a penalty for withdrawing the umbilical faster than the closure ramp, with electronics stockpile shelf life as a plausible mechanism. At n=60n=60 per point it does not estimate a stable response curve or its steepness.

Allocation-policy robustness. The results above could in principle be an artifact of the myopic one-step maximin allocator — a forward-looking operator might accept lower current worst-case growth to build future capacity. Because the dynamics and balances are linear, the finite-horizon LP is solved exactly — though receding-horizon control remains an approximation to full-horizon optimization (truncation and terminal-value effects persist; an investment paying off after year six is invisible to a six-year window). On paired draws (identical parameter samples per policy, shocks off), a six-year receding-horizon maximin reproduces the myopic policy essentially exactly — 16/30 vs 16/30 sampled runs expanding on the lunar surface, 11/30 vs 11/30 in LEO, with co-binding shares computed under the same finite 1% response definition as the baseline. The absolute level is not stable at this small paired n — the lunar count has swung across equally valid regenerations, so the policy equality is the stable finding, not the level. The agreement holds because the maximin criterion already directs each step’s investment at the worst-off sector, which is the future bottleneck. A third policy, maximizing aggregate growth subject to no sector shrinking, collapses (0/30 in both architectures): worst-case allocation is load-bearing, not incidental. Bottleneck-first heuristics are subsumed by the maximin construction itself. The defensible conclusion is correspondingly scoped: under paired, shock-free draws for the tested LEO and lunar central cases, a six-year receding horizon did not materially change the outcomes; global allocation-policy robustness (longer horizons, perfect foresight, robust control under shocks) is not established — and the retooling analysis of Part IV exhibits one regime where allocation family genuinely matters. (policies.py; paired-draw comparison in outputs/report_deep.md.)

Scalar-anchor sensitivity screening — with its scope stated. The claim that the strategic-material gap and logistics penalty dominate is a computation, not an assertion, and it is a scoped one — central assumptions, lunar architecture, shocks off, scalar anchors only; it does not rank structural requirement-matrix uncertainty, policy choices, shock distributions, or interaction effects, and repeating it across environments and sets with interaction-capable methods remains open cross-environment work: Spearman rank correlation between each anchor’s shared draw and the worst-case growth rate at year 30 across the ensemble (n = 300, central/ lunar, shocks off; anchors are drawn independently, so per-anchor rank correlation needs no independence corrections beyond the null band of roughly ±0.11, wider under multiplicity). Two parameters tower above the band: the space-electronics closure fraction (ρ ≈ +0.80) and the space logistics penalty (ρ ≈ −0.48) — both ASSUMPTION-class, which is the epistemic point: within this scalar screen, variation in year-30 growth is dominated by exactly the two numbers no one has measured. Every other screened anchor sits at or near the null band. (montecarlo.sensitivity; ranked table in outputs/report_deep.md.)

Integrated seed and aggregate-capacity results. The new layer is a second, explicitly assumption-class model, not a relabeling of the inherited balanced-capacity runs. Structurally it is a two-stage hybrid: a multisector, multi-material seed-sizing LP, followed by sector-resolved capacity-growth dynamics. All 18 sector capacities retain their own commissioning lag, ramp, and depreciation; the continuous operating-cell equivalent is derived as the slowest normalized operating sector rather than advanced as the state. The published central trajectory orders balanced seed-composition packets for continuity, while diagnostics compare independent maximin-sector, surplus-preserving, shock-aware, and perfect-foresight allocation. Failures enter explicit repair queues whose return to service consumes parts, repair service, intervention capacity, and time. Construction and commissioning are cohort-resolved. A scenario is LP-feasible when the seed LP admits a solution satisfying every material, service, autonomy, intervention, and throughput constraint over the scenario horizon. The doubling metric is first passage to two operating-cell equivalents — a continuous aggregate crossing, not a discretely commissioned second factory. The year-40 and terminal-window endpoints are separate. Central deterministic scenarios and deterministic 200-draw assumption ensembles:

bootstrap architecture central minimum-mass installed seed Earth strategic-material import stock (share of seed) aggregate operating-capacity doubling, 80-year extension sector-balanced cell-equivalents, year 40 design-space occupancy (LP-feasible / 200) feasible-draw seed p10 / p50 / p90
terrestrial closure rehearsal 206.7 t 48.1 t (23%) — 0.47 83/200 171 / 201 / 228 t
lunar strategic-material bridge 216.7 t 58.1 t (27%) — 0.54 126/200 181 / 212 / 247 t
strict lunar-only infeasible — — — 0/200 —
Moon–asteroid network 185.5 t 0.0 t 34.75 yr 3.61 187/200 155 / 204 / 310 t

The occupancy column is a count under the declared log-uniform sampling measure. It is not a calibrated probability, posterior, or empirical success rate.

“Minimum-mass installed seed” is the LP’s installed-equipment boundary, not delivered cargo. A separate deployment model adds packaging, unloading and site equipment, calibration references, initial spares, and startup-energy storage, then tracks delivered, staged, installed, commissioned, failed, recovered, and operating mass. Under those declared assumptions the 216.7 t lunar-bridge seed is 303.3 t delivered and reaches full operation at about 5.8 years. The LP result remains conditional rather than a global optimum over unknown processes or designs. A composition-changing Pareto search now varies process route, redundancy, and source portfolio; its 36-point frontier is a design-space diagnostic, not a claim that the enumerated alternatives are exhaustive. The import-stock share is worth stating plainly: at 27% of installed mass, the central lunar bridge is a substantially Earth-provisioned seed whose local loop supplies bulk mass, not a nearly closed system with trace imports. The year-40 column carries the crossing-versus-retention distinction: neither the terrestrial rehearsal nor the lunar bridge ever reaches sector-balanced doubling in the 80-year extension, and their compute sectors fall to 0.47 and 0.54 equivalents at year 40. The Moon–asteroid case crosses two at 34.75 years and reaches 3.61 at year 40 while expanding. The strategic import stock’s composition is resolved in outputs/integrated/tables/import_stock_composition.csv: Ni, Cu, and C dominate at roughly 80% of the lunar-bridge stock, with initial-rate coverage near five years per category.

The strict lunar-only case is a structural infeasibility, not a sampled tail: the central LP is infeasible — the configured trace-material yields cannot supply the assumed electronics and process-equipment stack — and all 200 draws preserve that infeasibility, so 0/200 restates the structure rather than measuring an uncertainty. Substitution, a different electronics stack, a new refining route, or a richer measured deposit can change it; the result is not a proof that lunar-only industry is impossible. The Moon–asteroid case assumes a deliberately synthetic composite portfolio rather than a known accessible body: 187/200 states what a sufficiently diverse source network would have to supply, not that such a portfolio is accessible, jointly recoverable on the assumed timetable, or economical. In its central solution the Moon supplies 366.2 t/yr of feed and the asteroid portfolio 173.8 t/yr. Source occurrence [S51–S56] bounds plausibility; it does not validate recoverable yield, reserve, throughput, purity, or transfer cost.

Terminal-window, ablation, and frontier diagnostics (r4.0). Five analysis passes interrogate the same declared architecture without introducing any new coefficient (machine-readable tables in outputs/integrated/tables/; all regenerate with scripts/run_integrated.py):

  • Sector resolution invalidates the scalar crossing result. The terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases are contracting (−0.022 and −0.027 equivalents over years 35–40), never cross two in the 80-year extension, and are bottlenecked by compute at year 40. The Moon–asteroid network crosses two at 34.75 years, reaches 3.61 at year 40, and is expanding (+1.530); advanced logic/memory is its slowest normalized sector. Machine-readable 40/60/80-year endpoints are in long_horizon_endpoints.csv, and the full 18-sector state is in sector_capacity_trajectory.csv.
  • The dynamic intelligence coupling is regime-dependent. The terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases are material-limited in 145/160 and 146/160 quarterly steps, and zero/freeze ablations move their endpoints by less than 0.1%. The source-diverse network is material-limited in only 48/160 steps: removing both coupling channels reduces year-40 balanced capacity from 3.61 to 2.70, or 65% of baseline net growth. This does not validate the coefficients; it shows that the implemented feedback becomes operative only after the stipulated source vector relaxes material supply. The starting AI level also binds statically: re-sizing at base autonomy makes the bridge and network seeds infeasible. The exhaustive primary-cap classification assigns the remaining 14, 15, and 112 steps respectively to the declared gross order-rate cap; live service capacity is never the primary dynamic cap (dynamic_regime_summary.csv).
  • Scaling is not redesign. Installing scaled copies of the minimum-mass composition does not rescue the terrestrial or lunar bridge case by year 40. In the Moon–asteroid case, the 1.0×, 1.25×, 1.5×, and 2× seeds reach the first additional balanced equivalent at 34.75, 33.75, 33.0, and 32.0 years. This sweep does not choose a different sector mix.
  • Relabeling the LP objective is also not redesign. Lexicographic solutions for minimum installed mass, minimum Earth-import mass, and minimum intervention demand return the identical capacity vector in all three LP-feasible central scenarios. The current variables expose no tradeoff for those objectives to choose. A genuine Pareto front requires alternative process routes, redundancy, sector composition, or deployment decisions. The separate robust-seed search supplies those choices and reports dominated and non-dominated designs (seed_objective_comparison.csv; robust_seed_pareto.csv).
  • Failure reasons and binding constraints are per-draw. Infeasible draws split between the autonomy threshold and the material LP (terrestrial 77/40, bridge 54/20, strict 33/167); feasible draws bind most often on Cu, C, Ni, and Cr (terrestrial and bridge) and on dopants plus refining and asteroid-transport throughput (network). The scalar-state claim that depreciation correlated positively with year-40 capacity is not retained: sector resolution makes depreciation and lag multipliers strongly negative against balanced year-40 capacity. The rank screen remains local to the declared independent multiplier measure, not a causal or global sensitivity result.
  • The strict-lunar cut is quantified. An elastic relaxation of the exact seed LP names the unsatisfiable rows and their minimum shortfalls over the horizon: Ni 19.0 t, Cu 18.4 t, C 15.3 t, Co 3.6 t, Cr 3.1 t, rare earths 2.3 t, Li 2.3 t, H 0.2 t, and dopants 0.1 t. The infeasibility is a distributed material cut, and the table doubles as the engineering target list any lunar-only architecture claim would have to defeat.

The coupled run distinguishes installed compute from the slowest-sector industrial aggregate. At year 40, the Moon–asteroid scenario has 5.82 normalized total endogenous compute capacity while its balanced aggregate is 3.61; compute is now its own sector rather than a copy of the scalar cell count. The run exports 0.78 normalized units to orbit. Constant-rate Earth-fed orbital deployment reaches 1.56, 2.81, or 4.99 units under the tight, base, and responsive rate cases. Those curves show the difference between rate-limited deployment and endogenous capacity growth under the configured coefficients; they do not forecast datacenter capacity.

The stateful debris stress test reports the five-year fragment creation-to-clearance ratio RdebrisR_{\mathrm{debris}} — fragments created divided by fragments cleared over the final five years, a flow ratio rather than a branching-process reproduction number:

deployment topology / mitigation creation-to-clearance ratio, last 5 yr fragment index, year 40
Earth-fed orbit / weak 0.61 1.602
Earth-fed orbit / strong 0.35 0.284
dense endogenous / weak 4.79 3.840
dense endogenous / strong 4.45 2.214
distributed endogenous / sparse topology 1.00 0.000

A ratio above one means only that more fragments were created than cleared in the window; it is not a cascade threshold. Strong mitigation lowers the dense case’s fragment index (3.84 → 2.21) and its flow ratio (4.79 → 4.45), but neither output establishes shell safety. The sparse case reads exactly 1.00 with an empty stock because realized clearance is capped by the fragments available — a zero-stock boundary, not a computed equilibrium — and it reaches that boundary only under an assumed 0.01 collision-kernel multiplier. The result supports topology as a co-designed industrial constraint; it does not establish a safe orbit, validate a debris environment model, or locate a cascade threshold. Complete tables and figures are generated from the same run in outputs/integrated/.

What Part I establishes and does not. It establishes structure: which sector binds, what the minimum cut is, how locations differ qualitatively (lunar fastest-doubling but hostage to the electronics cut; LEO feed-constrained but recycling-viable; Mars most path-dependent and import-fragile — the analysis drops the earlier “most robust per unit of assumption-optimism” ranking, which had no defined normalization), and where the feasibility margin lies — structure that survives the allocation-policy variation above. The integrated layer additionally establishes which declared material, autonomy, gravity, source, and commissioning constraints explain its own seed scenarios. Neither establishes point feasibility: both requirement matrices, element recipes and yields, strategic-material gap, repair efficiencies, stockpiles, autonomy coefficients, lags, source portfolio, and shock/debris rates are ASSUMPTION-class. Solar-array, regolith, sample, or satellite data do not establish the coupled behavior of mines, bearings, machine tools, electronics production, or dust-exposed radiators.

I.9 Development path, annotated

  1. Terrestrial autonomous-closure rehearsal. Before launch, operate an integrated seed factory on Earth using only the material forms, energy intermittency, communications constraints, spares allowance, and production methods intended for the lunar deployment. Exclude routine human entry; route every human intervention through a logged maintenance interface; inject equipment faults and communication outages; and require the system to manufacture, assemble, calibrate, and commission a second production cell. This stage does not reproduce lunar gravity, vacuum, radiation, or abrasive dust, so environmental qualification remains separate. It does test whether the industrial graph and its encoded operating knowledge are autonomous enough to export. Report intervention hours per machine-hour, imported mass per unit of added local capacity, critical bill-of-material lines producible, autonomous recovery fraction, time to a commissioned second cell, and every remaining single-point dependency. The r4.0 execution contract in params/rehearsal_protocol.yaml fixes the boundary, typed event schema, ten binary gates, threat-complete fault campaign, 30-day retained-cell test, and parameter-replacement rules. Its generated matrix remains entirely execution_pending or data_pending; it is a protocol, not a result.

  2. Earth-dependent operations. Earth supplies vehicles, energy systems, consumables, spares, electronics, and nearly all machinery; space assets perform narrow missions.

  3. Local-resource supplementation. Local water, oxygen, shielding, construction feedstock, and selected propellant inputs reduce imported mass without yet closing the industrial loop.

  4. Heavy-industry closure. The network produces bulk metals, glass, ceramics, structural parts, tanks, simple mechanisms, roads, pads, and large power structures.

  5. Advanced-manufacturing closure. It adds motors, actuators, sensors, precision tools, robots, spacecraft subsystems, computers, and factory machinery. Terafab is best read as a terrestrial rehearsal of this stage (Part III.2): advanced-manufacturing integration practiced on Earth before any attempt to export it.

  6. Self-sustenance. Internal production replaces depreciation and failure across every mission-critical category; Earth supply becomes optional rather than load-bearing.

  7. Self-expansion. The system builds more mines, refineries, factories, power systems, robots, transports, and compute than replacement requires.

  8. Intelligence-industry recursion. Additional compute improves intelligence; improved intelligence raises industrial replication efficiency; higher output creates still more compute.

    I increases → replication efficiency increases → infrastructure increases → compute increases → I increases

The bridge economy maps onto the ladder: terrestrial products carry the early stages; launch and connectivity carry Stages 2–4; orbital compute is a candidate Stage 4–5 tread; and in-space industrial services carry Stages 5–6. The model adds stage warnings. The Stage 4→5 transition is where the strategic-material gap binds — no amount of Stage 3 bulk closure substitutes for an electronics tier. Stage 5 is location-dependent: LEO requires a sustained capture-and-recovery feed loop; under the present 5% capture assumption, recycling is valuable but not knockout-indispensable at central values. Mars requires electronics stockpiles engineered to synodic shelf life or a local electronics tier. The lunar surface has the fastest conditional balanced-doubling pathway when electronics closes sufficiently; LEO has the more sustained central endpoint under its continuing-capture assumption.

Location sequence and the lunar hybrid. The development ladder is not a ladder of orbital altitudes. In particular, Sun-synchronous orbit is a planet-centered orbit whose plane precesses to preserve approximately the same local solar time [S49]. The familiar dawn-dusk SSO is still LEO—the 650 km orbital-compute design assessed in Part II is an example—not the destination after a lunar surface base.

For closure, the more coherent topology is:

  1. LEO as a bridge, not the terminal reservoir. Communications, observation, early compute, assembly demonstrations, and transport can earn revenue and test systems, but bulk growth remains exposed to finite imported/captured feed and density-dependent collision risk.
  2. Lunar surface as the material backbone. Extraction, bulk refining, construction, durable storage, shielding, and long-life machinery use a physical foundation and local regolith. South-polar planning seeks the conjunction of long illumination intervals and access to shadowed volatile deposits, while leaving reserve size and extraction economics unresolved; dust and landing ejecta remain major surface penalties [S47].
  3. Sparse lunar/cislunar orbit as the service layer. Communications, navigation, observation, reusable transports, depots, assembly, and selected compute occupy orbit only where zero-g or illumination benefits repay shielding, stationkeeping, and service costs. NRHO is a candidate gateway geometry designed for eclipse avoidance and low stationkeeping, not a substitute ore body or a passive maintenance-free base [S48].
  4. Distributed heliocentric expansion after lunar export closure. Productive nodes then spread across separated Sun-orbiting trajectories and resource paths—potentially including near-Earth objects—rather than reproducing one dense shell. The point is diversity of orbital elements and feedstocks, not one privileged “solar orbit.” Moving inward raises solar flux but also heat-rejection, radiation, communications, and materials constraints, so no optimal solar radius is claimed.

Material-source sequence. The Moon is not chemically equivalent to Earth, but neither is it short of bulk machine-building elements. Its crust is dominated by oxygen, silicon, magnesium, iron, calcium, and aluminum, with smaller titanium-bearing and other phases; composition varies strongly between highlands and mare terrains [S51]. Those elements support oxygen, glass and ceramics, aluminum, iron-bearing alloys, silicon feed, shielding, structures, and many bulk machine parts, subject to extraction energy, purification, alloying, yield, and process-equipment constraints. The early system can therefore treat the lunar surface as a bulk-material backbone while importing low-mass, high-criticality material vitamins from Earth: advanced chips, dopants, catalysts, specialty chemicals, bearings, sensors, precision tools, metrology, and any alloying elements whose local recovery is not yet viable.

An order-of-magnitude inventory check prevents “no iron” from becoming a false premise. At an average regolith bulk density near 1.5 t/m³ [S52], one square kilometer excavated to one meter contains about 1.5 million tonnes of regolith. Applying the approximately 3 wt% iron reported for lunar highlands material [S53] gives roughly 45,000 tonnes of iron in place. This is an illustrative inventory, not an ore reserve: it says nothing about site homogeneity, mineral form, excavation losses, energy, recovery yield, environmental impact, economics, or how much is practically extractable. It does show why asteroid mining is not a prerequisite for initial lunar iron.

The harder question is diversity. Lunar carbon and nitrogen occur at low concentrations in returned fines, while polar water evidence remains spatially heterogeneous and does not yet provide a bankable reserve estimate [S54, S55]. A robot-only ecology avoids agricultural and biosphere-scale demand, but it still uses volatiles and specialty elements for propellant, reduction chemistry, cooling, lubrication, polymers, process gases, electronics, and high-performance alloys. Carbonaceous asteroids and differentiated metal-rich bodies can eventually add water, carbon-bearing material, nickel, cobalt, and other feedstocks; returned Bennu material confirms carbon-rich organics and a history of water-related mineral chemistry in at least one carbonaceous body [S56]. Asteroids are therefore modeled as a follow-on route to diversity and supply sovereignty, not invoked as the first source of every machine metal.

Current demonstrations make individual conversion paths more concrete without closing the system. NASA describes integrated autonomous processing of regolith simulant into silicon solar cells, aluminum wire, oxygen, iron, and slag, alongside vacuum tests of molten-regolith electrolysis [S57]. These are meaningful subsystem demonstrations; they are not a lunar mine, an operational supply chain, a factory reproducing its own equipment, or an audited second production cell.

This ranks functions, not prestige destinations. Surface and orbit are complements: orbit is the transfer and service network; the surface supplies bulk matter and shielding. The inherited ten-sector and Part II models cannot compare that hybrid directly: they isolate lunar-surface capacity, cislunar compute, and Earth-supplied lunar compute, and they aggregate elements into industries. The integrated layer adds material-category bills of material, source yields, Earth–Moon–orbit–asteroid arcs, and aggregate endogenous debris states. It therefore computes an explicit hybrid scenario, but its recipes, yields, transfer capacities, composite asteroid source, and collision kernels are declared assumptions. It does not establish lunar material sufficiency, a recoverable reserve, a launch date for asteroid supply, or an orbital safety case.

I.10 Binding bottlenecks and failure modes

With model annotations:

  • Lithography and fabrication equipment — the named residual chokepoint one layer below foundries, and the deepest single closure problem in this framework.
  • Reliability and repair — the model makes mean-time-to-repair and spares closure first-class: repair is an explicit sector with an efficiency and a spares bill.
  • Thermal management — radiators are launched mass; Part II’s radiator axis.
  • Energy storage and continuity — the lunar night storage mass term; Mars dust-storm shocks.
  • Resource quality — LEO has no ore body, so the sustained capture-and-recovery feed loop binds even though the separately modeled recycling sector is not knockout-indispensable at central values.
  • Verification and control — Part III.4.
  • Political and legal environment.
  • Economic survival of the transition — Part II.1.
  • Concentrated coordination — single points of failure a distributed competitor lacks.
  • Paradigm-shift stranding — Part IV.3; exposure concentrated in the fabrication layer, while the fleet self-insures through its own 3–6-year depreciation.

Part II — Comparative Economics

II.1 The bridge economy

Each stage of the recursion must be independently profitable or deliberately financed: a staircase of self-supporting steps, not a single leap to closure. The plausible treads, in order: terrestrial products of the same machinery (vehicles, storage, robots — the ground floor pays rent and turns the autonomous seed into an audited industrial experiment); launch and connectivity (Starlink revenue and launch services fund transport); orbital compute services — a candidate tread, now priced rather than merely doubted (II.2–II.4); and in-space industrial services at higher closure. The test of the staircase: at every stage, revenue plus strategic financing must exceed the burn required to reach the next stage before the clock-setting components of Part I.4 expire — and Part I.8 makes the clock concrete: the electronics stockpile shelf life against the import ramp.

Stage 0 has a second economic role. Building the candidate lunar industries first on Earth captures process knowledge, failure data, tool interfaces, simulation residuals, and commissioning procedures while the repair economy is still accessible. Selling terrestrial output can finance that learning, but the decisive deliverable is the measured ability to build and commission a second cell under lunar-palette and no-routine-entry constraints. A factory that is profitable yet requires tacit human rescue has not validated the exported loop.

II.2 The crossover model

Unit: dollars per frontier-equivalent kilowatt-year of delivered IT load — defined as one kilowatt-year of IT electrical load powering accelerators of frontier-generation efficiency, delivered at the case’s utilization; older-node capacity is converted by its J/FLOP penalty, so a frontier-equivalent kilowatt-year buys the same computational output regardless of which hardware generation supplies it. Three reference cases: a LEO inference service; high-orbit/cislunar batch compute; and Earth-supplied lunar-surface compute, with local manufacture entering only through the closure sweep. Mass and power budgets resolve from anchored ranges — launch price sheets (company_statement), flexible-array specific power and deployable-radiator specific mass (technical_report), accelerator system cost and lives (reporting), DC capex, PUE, WACC (reporting), qualification multiplier and utilization (ASSUMPTION, evidence-tempered) — each with a source class and per-run provenance. The space cost is affine in launch $/kg, so break-even launch prices are exact. Chip efficiency is a first-class parameter: off Earth, every watt not computed must be radiated, and radiator, PV, storage, and structure are launched mass, so a FLOPS/W advantage scales the entire power side per unit of delivered compute — efficiency and launch price enter the crossover multiplicatively, with a quantitative refinement below. This makes the popular framing of orbital compute as a launch-price race incomplete and supplies a thermodynamic rationale for internalizing chip design, not merely fabrication or supply security: the most efficient accelerator can tolerate a higher launch price because it carries less power and heat-rejection mass per useful computation.

Two lifecycle architectures are reported separately:

  • Integrated disposable satellite: compute, PV, radiator, storage, structure, and original launch spend retire together.
  • Serviceable/reusable platform: the compute payload refreshes on its hardware life while the power/thermal/structure platform and its original launch spend amortize over a longer infrastructure life. This is an explicit scenario assumption; modularity alone does not demonstrate serviceability.

For WACC rr, useful life TT, and annual operations fraction fof_o,

CRF⁡(r,T)=r1−(1+r)−T,a(T)=CRF⁡(r,T)+fo. \operatorname{CRF}(r,T)=\frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-T}}, \qquad a(T)=\operatorname{CRF}(r,T)+f_o.

Let ChC_h be qualified accelerator capex, CIC_I the sum of PV, radiator, and storage capex, MhM_h accelerator mass, MIM_I launched non-hardware mass after local closure, μ\mu the destination launch multiplier, pLp_L the LEO launch price, and UsU_s delivered utilization. The complete space expression is

Ls=Cha(Th)+CIa(TI)+pLμ[Mha(Th)+MIa(TI)]Us=α+βpL. L_s = \frac{C_h a(T_h)+C_I a(T_I) +p_L\mu[M_h a(T_h)+M_I a(T_I)]}{U_s} =\alpha+\beta p_L.

The integrated-disposable case sets TI=ThT_I=T_h. The serviceable/reusable-platform case sets TI=max⁡(TI,anchor,Th)T_I=\max(T_{I,\mathrm{anchor}},T_h). For Earth scenario ee, PUE ψe\psi_e, electricity price pep_e, data-center shell capex CDCC_{DC}, utilization UEU_E, and frontier-equivalent node penalty ϕe\phi_e,

LE=ϕe[Ch,eCRF(r,Th,e)+CDCCRF(r,15)+8760peψe]UE. L_E = \frac{\phi_e\left[ C_{h,e}\operatorname{CRF}(r,T_{h,e}) +C_{DC}\operatorname{CRF}(r,15) +8760p_e\psi_e\right]}{U_E}.

The responsive Earth case evaluates frontier and older-node hardware and selects the lower LEL_E. Because LsL_s is affine in launch price, the exact break-even is

pL*=LE−αβ; p_L^*=\frac{L_E-\alpha}{\beta};

a negative value means non-launch costs alone exceed the Earth counterfactual.

For the central LEO serviceable-platform case, Ch=$63,640/kWC_h=\$63{,}640/\mathrm{kW}, CI=$1,697/kWC_I=\$1{,}697/\mathrm{kW}, Mh=17.3M_h=17.3 and MI=28.8kg/kWM_I=28.8\ \mathrm{kg/kW}, pL=$2,366/kgp_L=\$2{,}366/\mathrm{kg}, ah=0.3237a_h=0.3237, aI=0.1704a_I=0.1704, and Us=0.786U_s=0.786. Substitution gives

Ls=63,640(0.3237)+1,697(0.1704)+2,366[17.3(0.3237)+28.8(0.1704)]0.786=$58,264/kW−yr. L_s = \frac{63{,}640(0.3237)+1{,}697(0.1704) +2{,}366[17.3(0.3237)+28.8(0.1704)]}{0.786} =\$58{,}264/\mathrm{kW\!-\!yr}.

A fourth, explicitly conditional Starmind AI1 disclosure scenario does not replace those references. SpaceX publishes a 150 kW peak / 120 kW average compute payload, 150 kW solar array, 70 kW/tonne vehicle efficiency, 110 m² liquid radiator, and deployed dimensions of 20 by 70 m [S38]. The model uses the array/average-load ratio of 1.25. Because the page does not say whether the 70 kW/tonne numerator is peak or average, aggregate vehicle mass is sampled over the derived 14.3–17.9 kg per average kW range and the direct disclosures retain company_statement provenance while the interpretation range is labeled ASSUMPTION. Radiator area, dimensions, redundant loops, shielding, and laser links are recorded but receive no invented mass or cost where none is disclosed. Hardware cost, qualification, life, achieved availability, and launch price retain the existing anchors.

The lifecycle split is explicit and assumption-class. AI1 publishes only aggregate vehicle mass, so the model first constructs the generic accelerator/PV/radiator/storage/structure mass budget and then scales every component by one common factor until its sum equals the sampled AI1 total. The resulting generic hardware-versus-infrastructure proportion assigns accelerator mass to the hardware refresh life and the balance to the infrastructure life in the serviceable case; the disposable case amortizes both on the hardware life. Capex is not inferred from vehicle mass: qualified generic accelerator capex is retained, while generic PV, radiator, and storage capex is evaluated at AI1’s disclosed 1.25 array-to-average-load ratio. The aspirational 10 kg/kW case uses the same proportional split. Neither that mass decomposition nor physical serviceability is disclosed by SpaceX; both are ASSUMPTION, and the serviceable AI1 and 0.76× boundary depend on them.

A fifth case is a deliberately optimistic, deterministic boundary rather than a new baseline: Starmind AI1 aspirational best case. It uses SpaceX’s formal ≥99% launch-cost-reduction target as $185/kg and the prospectus’s long-term 100 kW/t orbital-compute scaling assumption (10 kg per average kW) [S37]. Because the company does not publish achieved AI1 qualification cost, useful life, or compute availability, the case separately labels as ASSUMPTION the favorable existing model bounds: 1.2× qualification, seven-year hardware life, and 0.95 utilization. It is excluded from Monte Carlo. Treating a target and three selected favorable bounds as probability distributions would manufacture a spurious probability of success.

Post-IPO architecture calibration. The technical literature available by late July 2026 does not supply one new “correct” mass-to-power ratio. It separates three architectures that should not be blended into one Monte Carlo distribution. Turyshev’s independent 1 MW high-sunlight closure allocates 29.4 kg/kW to PV, storage, and radiators; fixed spacecraft functions raise the total to 34–59 kg/kW [S39]. This independently brackets the model’s 46 kg/kW central generic LEO case and supports its order-of-magnitude placement, although the model’s full component-corner envelope (about 25–91 kg/kW) is wider. AI1’s derived 14.3–17.9 kg/kW sits below that conventional envelope and remains a separate company-specification case. Below both are research architectures: an integrated solar-compute-radiator panel concept at about 8.9 kg/kW and a tethered inference architecture at about 5 kg/kW [S40]. Those figures are legitimate lower-bound scenarios, but depend respectively on kilometer-scale integrated arrays, unqualified vapor chambers, thin tandem PV and custom ASICs, or on long tethers, distributed deployment, shielding, station-keeping, and micrometeoroid tolerance. They are pre-prototype architecture claims, not evidence that the generic spacecraft prior should move to 5–10 kg/kW.

Thermal closure is a system, not a radiator-panel coefficient. NASA’s flight and mission studies distinguish 2.75 kg/m² ISS radiator panels from 8.8 kg/m² after fluid loops and deployment are included; a JIMO study estimated 5 kg/m² for the complete system. At 353 K radiator temperature, 0.86 emissivity, and a 173 K environmental sink, the cited sizing is about 1.4 m²/kW, implying roughly 7–12 kg/kW for the complete heat-rejection system [S43]. This supports the middle and upper part of the model’s 3–12 kg/kW range, but shows that its low end represents advanced emitters, not a demonstrated full stack of cold plates, pumps, transport lines, deployment, and controls.

AI1 makes the ambiguity visible. Its published 110 m² radiator for 120 kW average compute is 0.92 m²/kW of quoted area [S38]. If 110 m² is physical footprint and both faces emit, the mean flux is about 545 W/m²; a simple Stefan–Boltzmann balance using NASA’s emissivity and environmental temperature gives an ideal radiator surface near 332 K (59 °C). If 110 m² instead denotes total emitting area, the load is about 1,090 W/m² and the ideal surface approaches 391 K (118 °C). Both calculations omit solar and Earth view, degradation, nonuniformity, pumping power, and the chip-to-coolant-to-radiator temperature drop. The disclosure is therefore not thermodynamically impossible, but its area convention, coolant temperature, and full thermal-system mass are crossover-critical measurements.

The terrestrial counterfactual responds — the epistemic requirement the static comparison missed. Three scenarios: tight prices scarcity (the politics-binds branch: permitting and climate commitments hold); base takes the anchors; responsive prices induced supply at the cheapest permitted firm-power floor — nuclear PPA, or the politically conditional natural-gas floor at $0.04–0.06/kWh (CCGT under $1,000/kW, ~2-year builds [S35]) — with an older-node hardware option taken when it wins on compute-normalized cost. Aspirational launch targets are sweep axes except in the explicitly labeled deterministic best case above; they never enter the probabilistic baseline.

Starship V3/V4 aspiration, normalized. SpaceX’s June 2026 prospectus does not quote a V3 or V4 customer price or a vehicle-specific cost per flight. It states instead that fully reusable V3 is designed to carry 100 metric tonnes to orbit, that a future generation could reach 200 tonnes as soon as V4, and that mature Starship is intended to reduce the historical $18,500/kg cost benchmark by 99% or more [S37]. Exactly 99% implies $185/kg; “or more” implies a lower value. The table converts that formal aspiration and three more aggressive sensitivity cases into full-payload flight-cost equivalents:

LEO sensitivity case $/kg V3: 100 t full-load equivalent V4: 200 t full-load equivalent status
formal corporate aspiration ≤$185 ≤$18.5M ≤$37M derived from the stated ≥99% reduction; not a price quote
aggressive mature-Starship case $100 $10M $20M scenario axis
extreme fuel-like case $50 $5M $10M scenario axis
extreme lower case $30 $3M $6M scenario axis

The dollar-per-flight columns are arithmetic ($/kg × full payload), not company forecasts. They rise for V4 in the table because $/kg is being held constant while payload doubles. Holding flight cost constant gives the other useful comparison: a $10M flight is $100/kg on a full V3 and $50/kg on a full V4. Under-filled flights cost more per delivered kilogram; external customer prices can exceed internal marginal cost; and none of these figures includes a demonstrated cadence, reuse count, refurbishment burden, or capital-recovery schedule. This analysis therefore uses $185/kg as the traceable corporate aspiration, $100/kg as an aggressive case, and $30–50/kg only as an extreme fuel-like sensitivity band. All remain comparison axes; $185/kg also enters the quarantined deterministic best case, never the Monte Carlo.

Two financing caveats are deliberate modeling choices. Earth uses an 8–15% WACC range and space a separate 10–22% range. Qualification multiplier, service life, repairability, and utilization are still sampled as separate anchored quantities; the favorable corner likely has correlated engineering causes, so its deterministic result is a boundary rather than a joint probability claim. Calibration: the Earth base case works out to ≈$1.7/kWh, matching published accelerator rental rates.

Cost accounting — included and excluded. Included: IT hardware with qualification premium; PV, radiators, storage, structure and their launched mass (with cislunar/lunar delivery multipliers); pumping power, rejection temperature, chip-to-radiator temperature drop, environmental view factor, and a thermal-reliability mass margin; spacecraft bus, communications, ground network, program NRE, insurance, spectrum/regulatory cost, disposal, and residual value; capital recovery at the architecture-specific WACC with component-specific lives; compute-hardware replacement and its launch mass on the refresh cycle; an operations fraction for ongoing ground segment, downlink, and station-keeping; utilization derating; Earth-side DC capex, PUE, hardware refresh, and firm-power floors. Excluded: launch-site, landing, turnaround, and fleet infrastructure beyond whatever is implicit in the $/kg target; launch failure beyond the insurance proxy; collision externalities and constellation-replenishment logistics; tax treatment; and architecture-specific link budgets or regulatory outcomes. Turyshev’s independent inequality remains a useful cross-check: at 40 kg/kW, a terrestrial infrastructure allowance of $10,000–40,000/kW permits only $250–1,000/kg for launch and spacecraft build combined before communications, operations, utilization, and finite-life penalties [S39]. The net direction of the remaining exclusions is not claimed to be uniformly conservative. The reported multiples are stylized-architecture outputs with wide ASSUMPTION ranges; the robust conclusion is structural — which terms dominate — not the exact ratios.

All sixteen architecture/reference rows have zero sampled points below parity in 2,000 draws. This is a design-space statement under the declared sampling measure, not a confidence bound on real-world success.

AI1’s aggregate mass disclosure is material but not sufficient at the retained central values: it cuts launched mass from about 54 to 16 kg/kW and LCO from about $77,600 to $46,500/kW-yr, yet fixed non-launch costs still exceed Earth base (central break-even approximately −$3,460/kg). With the remaining anchors simultaneously favorable — qualification ×1.2, seven-year life, and 0.95 utilization — AI1 is 1.74× Earth at the central launch anchor, has no positive break-even launch price (approximately −$191/kg), and reaches 1.13× at $250/kg. Completing communications, bus, NRE, insurance, spectrum, disposal, thermal-margin, and financing terms therefore removes the formerly reported favorable-corner crossover.

The aspirational case makes that conditionality explicit. The two company numbers alone—$185/kg and 100 kW/t—still produce about $34,200/kW-yr, 2.33× Earth base when qualification, life, and utilization remain at their central values. Selecting the three favorable non-company bounds as well produces about $16,000/kW-yr, 1.09× Earth base. The earlier incomplete-cost form would have produced 0.76×; completing the system boundary reverses that result. All five favorable conditions must hold together, and the model assigns no probability to them.

The company’s own scale target exposes the feasibility burden. At 100 GW deployed annually and 100 kW/t, the flow is one million tonnes/year: 10,000 full 100-t V3 launches (27.4/day), or 5,000 full 200-t V4 launches (13.7/day), and roughly 833,000 AI1-sized 120-kW-average spacecraft. Even at $185/kg, launch cost alone is $185 billion/year before spacecraft manufacture. At the later AI1 page’s disclosed 70 kW/t, the same flow rises to 1.43 million tonnes and 14,286 full V3 launches/year. The current design is therefore 30% below the older 100 kW/t assumption; reaching it requires 43% more kW/t. Full rapid reuse, daily turnaround at unprecedented cadence, upper-stage recovery, fleet size, range capacity, and manufacturing are load-bearing. So are seven-year whole-system reliability and 95% compute utilization, neither published for AI1. Collision externalities, constellation replenishment logistics, and landing/turnaround infrastructure remain excluded, while terrestrial energy, chips, cooling, permitting, and construction can also improve. The prospectus itself identifies approvals and spectrum as dependencies and warns that better terrestrial energy could reduce the orbital advantage [S37].

The post-IPO review sharpens the lifetime interpretation. The model’s 10–25-year infrastructure life is defensible only if the power and thermal platform survives multiple accelerator generations and the compute payload can actually be exchanged, serviced, or economically separated. For an integrated, non-serviceable LEO vehicle, the relevant infrastructure life is instead close to the spacecraft or compute life—typically about five years in the studies reviewed here [S39–S42]. The serviceable-platform and integrated-disposable results above now expose both lifecycle readings. Shortening every component to five years is appropriate for an integrated vehicle, but too pessimistic once modular payload replacement is demonstrated. Platform reuse is a named architecture gate, not an innocuous amortization choice.

A negative break-even means fixed, non-launch costs alone exceed the Earth cost: at those draws no launch price, even zero, closes the gap. The structural finding: the crossover is gated by the space-qualification premium, equipment life, and utilization — not launch price alone. The generic-LEO crossover surface (launch $/kg × life × qualification × radiator × closure × chip efficiency) shows no ratio-below-1 region at published prices on any single axis, and near-parity only in the defined Starship aspiration cases ($185/kg formal; $100/kg aggressive; $30–50/kg extreme) combined with favorable values on at least two other axes. AI1’s disclosed aggregate mass is a multi-parameter architecture constraint rather than a single-axis point on that generic surface; it produces the conditional near-published break-even above while leaving no competitive draw in either lifecycle ensemble. At the central LEO architecture’s approximately 54 kg/kW, those prices correspond to initial launch expenditures of about $9,990, $5,400, $2,700, and $1,620 per installed IT kW, respectively, before annualization. They largely remove the current launch bill, but a negative break-even still means they cannot overcome the fixed qualification/life/utilization gap on their own. Lunar closure is the weakest lever: chips are never closed, so even 95% closure of non-chip mass leaves the lunar case roughly 15–30× Earth at published prices — still more than an order of magnitude from parity.

The mass-multiplier refinement: at anchored values a 2× FLOPS/W advantage buys only ~39% of the benefit of halving launch price (ratio 4.0 vs 3.2 at $3,000/kg, both from 4.5), because the hardware term — untouched by efficiency — dominates both mass and capex. “The compute tax outweighs the launch tax” [S34] becomes true only after the qualification premium and hardware $/kW fall; near-term, both taxes are subordinate to qualification and life.

II.4 External claim and independent-study checks

The public crossover claims are recorded as comparison targets (never inputs). The completed-cost model does not reproduce the stronger Google/Planet crossover claim, even at its favorable anchored corner; this converts the disagreement into an architecture- and accounting-wide, testable one. The post-IPO review of independent studies below then checks the model rather than merely restating corporate claims. One preliminary correction of the record, because this document earlier mis-stated it: the Suncatcher design study does not claim system-level parity. Its cost section states twice that it is not a full economic analysis and not a comprehensive economic feasibility study, and its comparison sets the amortised launch component alone (≈$810/kW-yr for a Starlink-v2-class mass-to-power ratio at $200/kg; $810–7,500 across satellite classes) beside terrestrial data-center electricity spend (≈$570–3,000/kW-yr), explicitly excluding infrastructure, building, and chip costs [S32]. That is a launch-cost feasibility marker — the finding that launch need not remain independently prohibitive — not a parity claim, and it is consistent with this model, which reproduces launch as a minor term. The crossover claim this model contradicts is the stronger reading in circulation [S34], not the study’s own.

  • The Google/Planet study (reported: crossover at $200–300/kg [S34]). At $250/kg with central anchors: space/Earth = 2.61 — no crossover. Under the favorable corner within anchored ranges (qualification ×1.2, 7-year life, 0.95 utilization, 3 kg/kW radiators): 1.26 — still no crossover. The disagreement is no longer localized to launch price or three performance inputs; the completed non-launch system boundary is load-bearing.
  • The Suncatcher design study [S32] describes an 81-satellite dawn-dusk sun-synchronous cluster near 650 km with terabit-class optical links (an 800 Gbps unidirectional bench demonstration against a stated ~10 Tbps per-link requirement) and a learning-curve projection of ≲$200/kg by the mid-2030s — itself conditional on roughly 370,000 tonnes of additional cumulative mass launched, on the order of 1,800 Starship-class flights averaging ~180 per year, which the authors call ambitious. Its engineering results should be read precisely (arXiv v2, 17 June 2026):
    • HBM was the most TID-sensitive subsystem — irregularities from ~2 krad(Si) against a ~750 rad(Si) shielded five-year requirement, with no hard total-dose failures to 15 krad(Si) — while core logic and on-chip SRAM were the most SEE-sensitive. The reported inference error probability is roughly one per three million inferences under the stated assumptions, with the effect on training explicitly reserved.
    • At ~150 rad(Si)/yr, a seven-year dose (~1.05 krad) sits below the ~2 krad irregularity onset — the radiation results support five-year TID survivability with margin and do not obviously contradict seven-year TID survival.
    • What they do not establish is seven-year system reliability: SEE-induced corruption, host interruptions, training sensitivity, thermal management, and whole-spacecraft failure remain unresolved, with orbital repair called impracticable and redundant provisioning proposed instead — a cost, not an absence of one. The COTS practice supporting a low qualification premium (unmodified accelerators flying on imaging satellites [S34]) demonstrates cheapness, not five-year reliability.

The independent checks localize four additional gates:

  • Conventional mass and economic closure. Turyshev closes PV, eclipse reserve, thermal rejection, fixed spacecraft functions, sustained communication, utilization, and finite life in a single framework [S39]. Its 34–59 kg/kW total independently brackets and supports the generic central mass at the order-of-magnitude level. Its more important result is the combined launch-plus-build ceiling: $250–1,000/kg at 40 kg/kW before communications and lifecycle penalties. Every additional $1,000/kW of communication or operations cost reduces that allowance by $25/kg. Current public launch prices consume more than the entire allowance before a spacecraft is built.
  • Low-mass architectures are conditional, not contradictory. The integrated-panel and tether studies reach 8.9 and roughly 5 kg/kW respectively [S40], demonstrating that mass is an architecture variable rather than a universal constant. Both target inference and both exchange conventional subsystem maturity for deployment, structural, thermal, and custom-silicon risk. They justify explicit stretch scenarios; they do not justify assigning conventional spacecraft a five-kilogram prior.
  • Inference and training are different products. Van Berkel compares a terrestrial 8,000-accelerator Clos fabric with orbital meshes: about 28,800 TB/s of terrestrial bisection bandwidth versus approximately 2.25 TB/s for a two-dimensional and 10 TB/s for a three-dimensional orbital mesh at 100 Gbps links, with network latency 150–450 times higher [S41]. Even much faster optical links do not remove multi-hop diameter and collective-communication latency. The appropriate early comparison is therefore per-satellite or loosely coupled inference, preprocessing, and communication-integrated edge work—not frontier distributed training. Training should receive a network-performance model, not an ordinary utilization scalar.
  • Small space-native nodes already have a different cost structure. The peer-reviewed HPCA microdatacenter study finds power and thermal systems dominate bespoke small-satellite TCO, while compute hardware can be less than one percent; energy-efficiency improvements can reduce TCO by about two-thirds and are up to 2.5 times more valuable in space [S42]. This is encouraging for 0.5–10 kW Earth-observation preprocessing, where data originates in orbit and downlink is avoided. It is not evidence that a megawatt terrestrial-substitution service has the same economics.

The broader policy cross-check reaches the same conditional result by a different route. A University of Virginia assessment reports a simplified five-year 1 GW case at $135.6 billion in orbit versus $16.6 billion on Earth under present-style assumptions; near-parity appears only when launch falls to $30/kg, satellite hardware to $10/W, specific power rises to 100 W/kg, sunlight availability to 80%, and degradation and GPU failure both fall to 1% [S44]. Its model omits GPU cost, financing, insurance, logistics, and downtime and should not be treated as a precise forecast. Its contribution is the joint-condition result: parity emerges from several simultaneous improvements, not from launch price alone.

Consequence for the staircase, stated within the model’s service definition: the modeled orbital architectures are not cost-competitive as substitutes for terrestrial frontier compute at the stated assumptions. That conclusion now has a workload boundary: it applies directly to per-node inference in the cost model, while the new network evidence makes frontier distributed training less favorable than the scalar model shows. It does not price differentiated orbital products (in-orbit sensor processing, sovereign or military demand, resilience niches), which could be profitable while losing the commodity comparison. What follows for the staircase is correspondingly bounded: commodity-scale deployment ahead of the enabling corner is strategic positioning or learning investment rather than substitute-compute profit — an observation Part III converts into a discriminating test.

The electrical comparison is also reported in workload-specific units so a kW-year is not silently treated as equivalent computational output:

central service case cost per million defined inferences cost per network-effective training kW-year
Earth base $3,197 $17,989
generic LEO, serviceable $16,902 $490,528
Starmind AI1, serviceable $10,138 $294,235

The inference denominator is an ASSUMPTION-class workload requiring a named model, latency, accuracy, batch, memory, precision, and availability envelope. The training denominator applies explicit central network efficiencies of 0.158 in space and 0.815 on Earth. These values expose the interconnect gate; they are not benchmark measurements.

II.5 Competition and the takeoff-speed assumption

Explicit assumption. This thesis is decision-relevant chiefly under a slow-to-medium AI takeoff. Under a fast software takeoff, incumbent compute and algorithms decide outcomes before any physical loop closes; the space complex becomes something the resulting intelligence builds afterward, not the path by which it arises. The prominent published bet on the fast branch [S35] argues automated AI research compresses AGI-to-superintelligence into roughly a year; this document’s program is the other branch, and the disagreement operates on priors, not on any evidence item below.

The system is not alone. China is the closest existing implementation of the terrestrial stages at national scale (solar, batteries, robotics, rare-earth refining, trailing-edge fabrication) lacking, for now, a reusable heavy-lift economy. Hyperscalers close the same inputs with capital rather than ownership — power agreements, custom silicon, supply contracts — which works until aggregate demand outruns what markets can scale. State programs hold ISRU roadmaps but iterate slowly.

Two corrections to the launch-chokepoint assumption, both cutting against a durable launch monopoly: payload cost-performance improved by two to three orders of magnitude over the decade against a smaller multiple for launch price [S34] — a crossover model treating launch as the primary axis mis-weights its own sensitivity analysis (borne out in II.3, where the crossover is not launch-gated); and chemical rockets are a local optimum — mass-manufactured vehicles, electromagnetic or kinetic launch, and mass drivers from a low-gravity surface (named in the fabrication initiative’s own material [S29]) would reset the launch axis rather than move along it.

Externally induced supply versus internally controlled reproduction. Expansion purchased through markets can pay stacked scarcity rents when demand outruns supply. Properly qualified: markets are not static — the right formulation is a race between demand growth and induced supply with multi-year capacity lags as the binding term, and whether internal replication beats inducing market expansion is a rate comparison (which is what the responsive counterfactual of II.2 implements on the power axis). A self-replicating base escapes mandatory dependence on external Earth markets — not economic allocation, opportunity cost, or internal pricing, which persist in any multi-firm or internally-priced closed ecology: expansion re-denominates from currency into materials, energy, and time. Two caveats: the entry ticket is still paid in dollars — the first self-replicating unit is bought, not grown, which is what the bridge economy exists to finance — and the logic predicts convergence, not uniqueness: every serious actor eventually verticalizes or plateaus; the durable advantage is the shortest hardware doubling time once everyone is. Historical reference classes calibrate “unprecedented”: Manhattan and Apollo peaked near 0.4% of GDP; British railway investment ran ~40% of GDP over a decade; wartime borrowing far exceeded either [S35]. Trillion-scale buildout is extreme but inside the envelope. The relevant question is therefore the relative rate, financing, and dependency structure—not escape from capital itself. The symmetric dynamic diagnostic gives both Earth and space endogenous investment and finds that physical space compounding does not become self-financing in either declared 40-year case.

Integration versus modularity (the Coasean resolution). Markets scaled semiconductors a billionfold through disintegration; why would this time differ? A firm’s boundary sits where internal coordination costs exceed market transaction costs [S25]. AI attacks the internal term (Part I.6) — but it attacks the external one too, improving supplier discovery, specification, contracting, monitoring, quality assurance, pricing, logistics, and modular interface design. The correct conditional is therefore that AI moves the efficient boundary toward integration only if it reduces internal coordination costs faster than it reduces interfirm transaction costs, an empirical question this document does not settle; what does survive is that the market interface retains an irreducible capital requirement efficiency gains do not remove. The defensible conclusion is bounded: AI may move the efficient boundary toward integration — not that ownership integration outperforms modular ecosystems in general. Three qualifications are central: markets also supply experimentation, selection, redundancy, and price signals, which an integrated complex must replicate internally or decay into soft-budget pathologies; technical closure (the network can produce its inputs) must not be conflated with contractual or ownership closure — this thesis requires only the first; and the in-domain integration success story confounds integration with reusability, cadence, and incentives [S1].

The operating wall. Physics-priced inputs (energy, materials, machine-hours) fall with scale; society-priced inputs (land, permits, interconnection, litigation, goodwill) rise with it — on Earth, closure has a structural ceiling because land, law, and neighbors cannot be internalized. Space shrinks and relocates the society-priced term rather than abolishing it, with one favorable property: permission attaches to the gateway (launches, spectrum) rather than the complex, so the millionth robot needs no new municipal permit. The hard physical version: Earth has a planetary waste-heat budget; space offers radiator area not bounded by a planetary surface (though still bounded by matter, transport, geometry, and maintenance — Part IV) — though not free rejection. Two external observations bracket how hard the wall binds now: data-center siting is already politically contested over electricity, water, and land — the society-priced curve observed from inside the industry [S34] — while the AGI-buildout literature meets the same wall with natural gas and deregulation at a firm-power floor below the nuclear PPA, never mentioning orbit [S35]. The wall binds through politics more than physics or long-run capital — though near-term hardware (turbines, transformers, cooling, construction capacity) can also bind — and the difference between branches is a parameter in this model, not a mood. And the sequence remains brutal: before high closure, space is the most expensive place to operate — every kilogram of spares travels at full launch freight while depreciation runs at its worst (II.3’s ~4–9×) — so the declining-cost regime switches on only after κ is high, which is why the bridge economy and the clock-setting components decide who survives to reach it.

The threshold-model argument. If RSI capability is a threshold — a base model good enough to run verified improvement loops — a smarter starting model confers a head start that the loop erodes; the durable variable becomes who runs more loops, which is hardware. Mid-2026 evidence supports continued benchmark compression between open and proprietary models (open-weight releases benchmarking near the frontier [S12]); it does not establish commoditization at an autonomous-R&D threshold, so hardware dominance is the small-α branch of the model rather than the established trajectory. If RSI-grade capability does arrive in open weights, model advantage weakens sharply without evaporating — post-training, proprietary data, evaluation systems, inference infrastructure, tool integration, operational reliability, distribution, and the capacity to run physical experiments all persist as differentiators — and to that extent the contest shifts onto the physical loop, the strongest form of the verticalization thesis. The counterpoint: the argument holds only if capability is threshold-like rather than continuously compounding (L_RSI ∝ Aα·Cβ·V^γ, with α unknown); benchmark convergence does not establish that autonomous R&D capability is threshold-like. And the structural counterweight: models converge because they train on the same public data, so residual differentiation concentrates exactly in proprietary physical-process data (Part I.2) — if general capability commoditizes, the model contest narrows to the domains where training data is generated by owned industry, folding the model race back into the physical loop.

Part III — Strategy Interpretation and Governance

III.1 A Musk-associated technology stack

The following mapping is an analytical interpretation of how existing companies could supply layers of the proposed system — not proof that they are managed as one program, although the 2026 developments (the Terafab initiative; SpaceX’s absorption of xAI) bind the transport, communications, intelligence, and fabrication layers by overlapping control, strategic coordination, and contractual collaboration. Tesla remains a separate public company; a shared controlling figure and a framework agreement are not common ownership (Form S-1 pp. 7, 10, 154) [S27].

layer contributor capability role in recursion
Intelligence xAI (within SpaceX) AI research, large-scale compute [S3] design, coordination, recursive digital improvement
Energy Tesla Energy generation, storage, power electronics [S2] power for compute, factories, robots
Robotic labor Optimus manipulation, maintenance; stated Terafab construction role manufactured labor capacity
Manufacturing Tesla high-volume factories, batteries, motors factory design, machine production at scale
Fabrication Terafab (Tesla, SpaceX, xAI; Intel from Apr 2026) declared: chip design, lithography operation, fabrication, memory, packaging [S6–S10, S27, S29] declared compute-substrate layer; framework stage
Transport SpaceX / Starship reusable heavy lift seed deployment, materials movement
Communications Starlink distributed connectivity coordination across remote nodes
Compute deployment planned D3 constellation radiation-tolerant silicon space-based compute as stated product
Data fleet, factories, test programs telemetry, process parameters, failure archives the physical loop’s exhaust (I.2)
Industrial knowledge Tesla / SpaceX / xAI / Terafab CAD/CAM, simulation, software toolchains, process recipes, material models, build records, and failure archives portable digital seed and industrial memory
Settlement Mars objective self-sufficient city as stated goal demand center; survival independent of Earth

The theoretical advantage is not ownership of complementary companies but a shorter verified end-to-end loop across design → manufacture → deploy → learn. The closure race rewards the shortest such loop, not the largest stock of any single input.

xAI improves intelligence → AI improves robots and factories →
factories expand energy and hardware → Terafab expands chips →
hardware expands compute on Earth and in orbit → compute improves AI

The advantage, if it exists, is the ability to integrate feedback, capital allocation, engineering, deployment environments, and industrial production into that shorter loop. Reported preparations for a SpaceX public offering would, if completed, add a financing event for the capital-intensive middle of the loop [S9, S27]; financing capacity is an enabler, not evidence of closure intent.

III.2 Terafab and the fabrication frontier

What was announced: a Tesla–SpaceX–xAI chip fabrication initiative (March 2026), joined by Intel in April; declared scope from chip design through lithography operation, fabrication, memory, packaging, and test; reported $20B initial plant with a filing-based ceiling near $119B; 2-nm target; mass production stated for 2028 [S6–S10]. What the primary source says [S27]: a general framework with Tesla — timelines, milestones, and capital expenditures for specific projects not yet determined and subject to separate agreements; a stated orbital data-center plan from as early as 2028; and an aim to alleviate potential future chip shortages for orbital AI (Form S-1 pp. 7, 10, 154). First-party messaging versus legal commitment [S29]: the initiative’s own site frames the effort on the Kardashev scale, publishes scaling figures (~1B robots, ~10 Mt/yr launched, >1 TW solar), names chip lines for vehicles, robots, and space (AI5, AI6, D3), publishes an explicit orbital-versus-terrestrial cost decomposition, and names lunar mass drivers as the next step. The divergence between site and filing is itself informative: a strongly space-oriented declared strategy resting on unsettled implementation.

The implementation detail matters. Reporting describes a roughly $3B research fab producing a few thousand wafers per month before any scaled phase, with ambitions moving from about 100,000 wafer starts per month toward one million [S6–S10]. Those figures evidence intended scale, not comparable output: wafer starts cannot be compared with a foundry’s global production without node, wafer diameter, product mix, yield, and effective die output. Planned products include AI5/AI6 chips for vehicles and robots and radiation-tolerant D3 silicon for orbital deployment; Optimus robots have been assigned a stated construction and operating role. Each remains a target rather than demonstrated capacity.

What it changes: fabrication moves from missing term to declared target; the residual dependency moves one layer down (EUV lithography, deposition, etch, metrology, ultra-pure feedstocks — sole-supplier equipment, not foundries); the fab-to-space link becomes explicit (D3). What it does not change: no wafers have been produced; the timeline is faster than any historical ramp; industry skepticism is on record.

The competence question needs stating precisely, since earlier drafts got it wrong: Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI have no advanced-fab operating record, but Intel plainly does, and the reported process plan is Intel 14A — so the open question is whether that experience transfers into this organizational structure and what obligations Intel has actually accepted, not whether anyone involved has run a fab.

Two further corrections. The sites are distinct: a smaller Tesla research fab at the Giga Texas campus, and a proposed SpaceX-led scaled facility in Grimes County whose county tax and economic-development agreements are now recorded as fully executed — strengthening site-level commitment without constituting a definitive construction, funding, or operating agreement [S6–S10]. And scale comparisons used in earlier drafts are withdrawn: wafer-start counts cannot be set against a foundry’s global output without controlling for wafer diameter, node, product mix, yield, and effective die output, and “one terawatt per year” is a claimed annual production rate of hardware whose aggregate nameplate power draw would total a terawatt — a manufacturing-throughput figure not commensurable with national electricity consumption.

The lithography question: for terrestrial operation, purchased lithography is an acceptable permanent dependency; for high space closure it must eventually be reproduced, substituted (older nodes at volume; nanoimprint; e-beam), or accepted as designed permanent import — the deepest single closure problem in this framework (and precisely where the Part I strategic-material gap lives). The analysis adds the bottleneck convergence: the AGI-buildout literature identifies advanced packaging and HBM memory as the near-term chip constraints [S35], and HBM is what the Suncatcher radiation testing found most dose-sensitive [S32] — the same component class is the terrestrial scaling bottleneck and the space reliability weak point.

Terafab-specific observables. The milestones that would change this assessment are: the first research-fab wafer and disclosed yield at any node; visible order flow from lithography, deposition, etch, and metrology suppliers; evidence that memory and advanced packaging are actually produced in-house rather than outsourced; radiation-qualified D3 silicon with disclosed orbital-compute unit economics; and definitive agreements that commit capital and counterparties. Industry skepticism is therefore a testable forecast, not a rhetorical counterweight [S10].

III.3 Competing hypotheses: the evidence table

The hypotheses are nested rather than exclusive, since a long-run off-world strategy can be pursued through vertical integration and supply hedging — those are mechanisms, not alternatives. H0 is the matched portfolio-adjacency baseline: projects may share ownership, branding, finance, suppliers, data, bilateral interfaces, and ordinary commercial or supply-security motives without sharing one off-world systems architecture. Standalone orbital compute, a domestic fab, launch/AI consolidation, and cross-selling are all H0-compatible. H1 adds deliberate coordinated space–AI–industrial development — the P4a claim — evidenced most strongly by shared technical interfaces, common architecture documents, binding cross-program milestones, cross-subsidy, or joint resource allocation, not by co-ownership alone. H2 adds an explicit intended transition to recursive industrial closure — the P4b claim — with closure metrics, a seed bill of materials, minimum-cut work, or locally reproducible production equipment as its distinctive observables. Because the hypotheses nest, each evidence item is assessed on two separate margins — does it separate H1 from H0, and does it separate H2 from H1 — and the assessments are ordinal, not numerical: the items are correlated (several derive from the same corporate communications), absence-items depend on assumed observability, and declared intent is cheap; assigning multiplicable likelihood ratios to such material would imply a probabilistic model that does not exist. Ratings: neutral (equally expected under both), weak, moderate, strong (difficult to explain under the alternative). A distinct motive reading cuts across the nest: heavy industry moves off Earth to protect the biosphere rather than escape a constrained platform [S34] — same physics, different telos — which supplies an additional non-H2 explanation for any orbital-compute observation. Per the propositions ladder, everything here concerns P4, and P3 is decoupled from it: the migration case requires no claim about any company’s intentions.
