E12 and E15 (the Google/Planet Suncatcher prototype program and the design study’s content) are removed from this table: they are actions of independent actors and bear on no hypothesis about the Musk-associated complex’s intentions. They are retained as engineering reference-class observations under external cross-checks below — an announced prototype program (satellites slated for early 2027 [S33]), and radiation results bounding the qualification corner (5-yr TID survivability supported with margin; 7-yr system reliability unresolved; II.4).

What the models add to interpretation. A rational H2 actor facing Part I would visibly invest in the electronics closure layer — rad-tolerant lines, stockpile logistics, shelf-life-rated spares, off-world packaging/test — because that is the most frequently observed minimum cut in the sampled ensemble. A rational H1-or-H2 actor facing Part II would run orbital compute at a loss for positioning, or privately believe the COTS/long-life corner; sustained scaled deployment after the unit economics are publicly evident is a moderate-to-strong discriminator between the strategic (H1/H2) and commercial (H0) readings — and conversely, quiet retreat after the demonstration phase is what H0 predicts. On-orbit materials-recovery recycling at scale (not debris-compliance servicing) would be moderate-to-strong for H2 specifically: Part I’s structural result that the LEO architecture lives on its recovered-mass feed loop (capture/mining receives ~98% of central co-binding credit; the analysis withdraws the stronger stale claim that the recycling sector was knockout-indispensable) makes building that loop the rational early move of a LEO-first closure strategy and of no one else.

External cross-checks [S35]: the canonical AGI-buildout analysis resolves the power wall terrestrially without mentioning orbit — non-space-interested corroboration of Part II from outside; its chip bottleneck converges with the space radiation weak point (III.2); and its fast-takeoff thesis, if right, weakens the H1/H2 rationale regardless of the evidence — an effect on the prior, reported separately from the item-level assessments. A provisional July 2026 frontier-lab hiring sweep is quarantined as an appendix note (A.7), not used as an evidence-table item or model input.

Cumulative assessment (ordinal synthesis, not multiplication — the items are correlated and the ratings judgmental): the evidence supports H1 at the level of declared direction but does not establish a coordinated technical architecture. The initiative list in the SEC-filed offering materials (E6) and the first-party messaging (E14) establish an off-world portfolio narrative, while E7/E9/E13 are consistent implementation steps; the matched H0 explains all of them through adjacent commercial, supply-security, financing, and promotional motives unless shared interfaces, milestones, or resource allocation appear. It does not establish H2: no item in the table is more than weakly diagnostic for closure intent, the closure-specific observables (seed bills of materials, reproduction metrics, minimum-cut roadmaps, locally reproducible production equipment) remain absent (E10), and most observed actions are equally expected under a conventional integrated off-world commercial strategy. P4a is documented; P4b remains inferential — which is exactly the split the propositions ladder now encodes.

III.4 Control and governance of a self-expanding system

A self-expanding autonomous industrial network is, formally, a governed macroscale von Neumann replicator; the property that makes it valuable — compounding physical replication — makes its failure modes compound too. Verification must scale with expansion (V is a safety term); throttle authority must be explicit (rate limits, hardware-level authorization of replication steps, clarity about who holds them); the legal frame is unsettled and first movers set precedent.

The framework resolves its own tension — celebrating escape from society-priced costs while requiring retained constraint — through the gateway: in space, permission attaches to launches and spectrum, which is where governance holds enforceable leverage. The leverage variable is dependency — but not proportional to (1 − κ), since this document has already established that scalar closure is invalid and a single low-mass import can be a minimum cut conferring disproportionate leverage. The governing quantity is G_dependency = f(criticality, substitutability, stockpile, supplier concentration, enforceability): what matters is whether withholding an input collapses the network, not how much of it is imported. Part I supplies an answer that is architecture- and parameter-conditioned, and must be stated that way: where import dependency remains load-bearing — the lunar and Mars ensembles — electronics is the most frequently observed minimum cut, and the strategic imported parts are the last material governance handle; in the sampled central LEO draws a single import line is fatal only in a minority of draws (~0–11% for electronics across deterministic regenerations), so there the material handle runs mainly through feed availability and the recovery loop rather than any one import line. Material-dependency governance has a declining window as closure rises; throttle authority, verification requirements, and replication limits are cheapest to embed as licensing conditions during the bridge period. Closure does not end governance (communications, cryptographic authority, personnel, ownership, insurance, treaties, orbital traffic, trade remain), but the material handle is the one that closes.

A serious control architecture — beyond this document’s scope but within its obligation to specify — requires hardware roots of authority; multi-party authorization for replication steps; explicit rate limits; compartmentalization and fault-containment zones; secure update and rollback channels; explicit cyberattack and insider-risk models; independent verification capacity; operator and government incentive analysis; jurisdiction and liability rules; and failure recovery when communications with Earth are unavailable. These are named requirements, not solved problems. They must be tested under the same loss-of-import, shock, and degraded-communications conditions used to test the production system.

Design principle: replication authority should be the most verified and least autonomous function in the system — positioned deliberately against the efficiency gradient, embedded at the seed stage, because it cannot be retrofitted onto a mature complex.

III.5 Falsifiable indicators, model-ranked

The indicators carry ordinal diagnostic ratings informed by the models (consistent with III.3’s refusal of numerical likelihood ratios; numerical likelihood-ratio language is intentionally excluded):

  1. A terrestrial autonomous-closure demonstrator that constructs and commissions a second production cell under lunar-palette, no-routine-entry constraints — strong for H2 over H1.
  2. Production or fabrication equipment explicitly designed for local extraterrestrial reproduction — strong for H2 over H1.
  3. A dedicated cross-company closure program with published κ-vector metrics — strong for H2 over H1 (flips E10).
  4. A machine-readable off-world seed package containing the physical bill of materials, digital toolchain, industrial memory, dependency graph, and experimental/commissioning plan — strong for H2 over H1.
  5. An element-resolved Moon–Earth–asteroid supply plan with source yields, recovery losses, transfer arcs, import-withdrawal milestones, and explicit strategic-material import stocks — strong for H2 over H1.
  6. Sustained scaled orbital-compute deployment despite publicly evident unfavorable unit economics — moderate-to-strong for H1/H2 over H0 (Part II makes the test operational — watch fleet growth after the economics are public).
  7. Electronics strategic-material-gap engineering: stockpile facilities, shelf-life-rated spares logistics, off-world packaging/test lines — moderate-to-strong for H2 over H1 (Part I makes it the rational first move of a closure strategy).
  8. On-orbit materials-recovery recycling at scale — moderate-to-strong for H2 (the Part I LEO feed-loop result; the sector-indispensability framing was a stale-output claim and is withdrawn, the indicator survives on the feed-dependence structure).
  9. An export-control-scoped internal model variant — moderate.
  10. Terafab executed definitive agreements with committed capital — weak-to-moderate (upgrades E7 from framework to program; hedging inside H0 still predicts it).

The ranking above asks which observations discriminate among H0, H1, and H2. A second set asks whether the physical thesis is becoming feasible at all. These lower-diagnosticity but still necessary indicators are retained:

  • robots performing unscripted maintenance, construction, mining, and machine tending for long periods, with autonomous recovery fraction and human intervention hours reported per machine-hour rather than described only as “limited”;
  • local production of propellant, structural material, and replacement parts at operational rather than laboratory scale;
  • factories using locally processed feedstock to manufacture additional power, extraction, and production equipment;
  • a measured decline in imported mass per unit of local productive capacity, reported by component class rather than as an aggregate mass fraction;
  • element-level closure reported as inputs, inventories, losses, recycled flows, and source-specific yields—not inferred from aggregate local mass;
  • space-manufactured compute, or production equipment capable of making it;
  • net positive industrial reproduction after depreciation — P > D in every indispensable sector — with published r and δ estimates by component class;
  • the Terafab-specific milestones in III.2: first wafer and yield, process equipment orders, in-house memory and packaging, qualified D3 silicon, orbital-compute revenue, and a measured robot reproduction ratio;
  • open-weight systems demonstrating sustained autonomous verified improvement loops — evidence for the threshold-like branch in II.5 — and, separately, fleet- and factory-owning actors outperforming open models on engineering tasks in a way attributable to proprietary process data; the contrary result would show that κ_D does not bind;
  • a sustained measured decline in cost per verified improvement loop, and replication-relevant conditions appearing in launch licenses or export-control terms while material leverage still exists.

Threshold observations that would move Appendix A: a demonstrated ISRU plant above ~50% full-system materials closure; audited robot production figures; an independent satellite-reliability audit reporting cohort-specific failures per satellite-year, separated from retirements and planned disposals (the earlier “~2.5–3%” figure was an early-cohort fleet fraction, not a general hazard rate, so divergence from it is not the right test); and any traceable datum on off-world-producible electronics tiers — the strategic-material-gap anchor this document flags as its highest-value currently parameterized missing measurement. The thesis weakens if humanoid robotics remains economically narrow, advanced manufacturing cannot be localized, launch costs stop declining, closure requires a permanently growing Earth supply chain, verification costs rise faster than capacity — or if Terafab devolves into design-and-packaging dependent on external front-end fabrication, which would reopen the fabrication term entirely.

III.6 Refined complete thesis

The coherent end state remains a recursively self-expanding space industrial ecology. Reusable rockets transport an initial seed. AI supplies scientific, engineering, and coordinating intelligence. Robots provide scalable physical labor. Local energy systems supply power. Mining and refining convert extraterrestrial matter into industrial feedstocks. Automated factories produce structures, machines, robots, transport vehicles, energy systems, and — if the electronics tier can close — compute. Communications integrate specialized nodes into one economic and operational network.

The network first reduces Earth dependence, then reaches self-sustenance, and finally produces net additional capacity. At high closure, station-keeping, collision management, maintenance, transport, and coordination remain real requirements; they are supplied by industries inside the network rather than purchased as externally scarce services.

matter + energy + intelligence + time → expanding productive capacity

Recursive self-improvement is therefore not limited to software. Intelligence improves the machinery and institutions that create intelligence; the industrial substrate returns energy, compute, data, experimentation, and physical agency to the intelligence layer. The ultimate product is an industrial system capable of producing more of itself.

The most precise formulation now available is conditional and model-separated. Current evidence documents deliberate integrated space–AI–industrial direction (P4a), but neither a shared technical architecture nor an intended transition to recursive closure (P4b). The inherited industrial model finds expansion under some assumption sets and failure under others, with electronics and feedstock dependencies localized by architecture. The new integrated-bootstrap model makes a first explicit pass through the complete intelligence–industry loop, seed bill of material, source network, and aggregate operating-capacity growth; it finds the lunar strategic-material bridge and the synthetic Moon–asteroid scenario LP-feasible under central assumptions and the configured strict lunar source graph structurally infeasible. Because every new structural coefficient is declared rather than measured, that is an executable hypothesis, not evidence that the complete recursion can be built. The comparative-economics model finds the Earth-dependent bridge uneconomic at anchored values and does not price the mature high-closure ecology. Capability accumulation is observed; positive off-world industrial reproduction and a unified closure strategy are not.

I(t+1)=I(t)+f(C,D,V,H),H(t+1)=H(t)+g(I,E,M,R)−δenvH(t),C(t+1)=C(t)+h(H,E,fab) \begin{aligned} I(t+1) &= I(t) + f(C,D,V,H), \\ H(t+1) &= H(t) + g(I,E,M,R) - \delta_{\mathrm{env}}H(t), \\ C(t+1) &= C(t) + h(H,E,\mathrm{fab}) \end{aligned}

The initial formulation left f, g, and h as unspecified placeholders and this compact model was a causal diagram. The inherited model operationalizes g as the lexicographic maximin allocation of Part I.7 (with repair, recycling, stockpiles, and imports) and decomposes δ_env by sector and environment. The integrated layer supplies a first stylized f and h: installed compute drives verified intelligence through a saturating gain law; intelligence raises task autonomy and industrial productivity; the resulting operating cells manufacture additional compute after construction and commissioning lags. Constant-rate Earth-fed deployment is run beside it as the counterfactual. These functions are executable and swept, but their coefficients are ASSUMPTION-class and they omit training data, algorithmic regime changes, verification failures, hardware-node detail, and many coordination limits. The model therefore tests the consequences of a coupling law; it does not measure that law or establish takeoff, subject also to the speed caveat of II.5. The r4.0 ablations sharpen this further: in the material-starved terrestrial and lunar-bridge cases, removing the dynamic coupling changes almost nothing; in the stipulated Moon–asteroid network it reduces year-40 net balanced growth by about 46%. The declared f and h therefore become operative only after the source vector relaxes material supply, while the starting AI level also matters through seed feasibility (I.8). This is a regime implication of assumed coefficients, not evidence that the coupling exists at the stipulated strength.

What the thesis does not claim

  • It does not establish that the companies are managed under one confidential master plan; III.3 assesses the public evidence.
  • It does not imply that energy, matter, infrastructure, coordination, or opportunity cost become literally free.
  • It does not assume intelligence automatically solves semiconductor fabrication, reliability, verification, governance, or safety.
  • It does not claim that the degrees of freedom of a current humanoid robot demonstrate unscripted industrial autonomy; embodied task coverage, recovery, and verification remain unmeasured requirements.
  • It does not require human settlement, agriculture, or a closed biosphere for the reference machine ecology, nor does it claim humans could never be present. A crewed architecture is a larger closure problem than the one modeled here.
  • It does not require every industrial node to be self-contained; closure can exist at network level.
  • It does not require uninterrupted exponential growth; the system can move through bottleneck-limited regimes and can double before later losing viability.
  • It does not claim Terafab will achieve viable yields or off-world fabrication closure; it is a declared terrestrial attempt whose implementation remains unsettled.
  • It does not claim a slow takeoff is certain; the physical-path thesis is conditional on the slow-to-medium branch in II.5.
  • It does not claim that closure is imminent, that model frequencies are empirical probabilities, or that space compute is economical today.

Part IV — Conclusion, and Speculative Terminal Scenarios

IV.1 The defensible core, restated with numbers attached

Two constraints, two rate comparisons, one passage. Externally induced supply expansion competes with internally controlled reproduction, while the operating envelope compares terrestrial social and infrastructure costs with off-world transport, reliability, and closure costs. Neither comparison is escaped by terminology; both remain conditional on surviving the bridge. The bridge’s failure mode is now specific: hold electronics-class stockpiles against shelf life, and reach local production of some electronics tier before the import ramp decays. The defensible core conclusion stops here, with its conditionals quantified: if industrial closure becomes sufficiently high across every indispensable sector (Part I’s bottleneck is architecture-specific: capture/mining dominates LEO, electronics dominates the Moon, and electronics and power co-bind on Mars) and terrestrial expansion costs rise faster than off-world deployment costs (Part II says: not at anchored values; only in the qualification/life/utilization corner at target-class launch prices), then some large-scale industrial and computational activity may migrate off Earth. Everything beyond that sentence is scenario.

QUARANTINE NOTICE. Sections IV.2–IV.4 are scenario-class: internally consistent extrapolation, not established result. Nothing in them feeds back into Parts I–II inputs. Each scenario carries a model check — usually a constraint, not support.

IV.2 After convergence: deployment as the terminal regime

At some point the marginal value of further design improvement falls below the marginal value of another deployed node — architectural convergence. Past it, intelligence behaves as a commodity produced by infrastructure — heuristically, throughput ~ deployed energy × physical efficiency, a relation that omits memory, interconnect, utilization, data, reliability, verification, latency, workload composition, and fabrication yield. Efficiency is floor-bounded (Landauer, with reversible logic the stated exception); scale plausibly becomes the dominant marginal variable rather than the only one; scale means energy; energy means collector area; and collector area is not bounded by a planetary surface off Earth. It remains bounded — by matter, transport, orbital geometry, heat transport, collision risk, maintenance, and control, and per the published cluster analysis by the quadratic scaling of satellite count with cluster radius and by mutual occlusion of rejected infrared between closely flown spacecraft [S32]. The ceilings-and-rates argument is retained in sensitivity form: the waste-heat ceiling sits perhaps two orders above current civilizational energy use, the thermodynamic floor several orders below current efficiency, and the ~3×/yr algorithmic-efficiency figure [S26] measures compute-for-fixed-language-performance only. Under sustained compounding, distances that look like centuries become decades — whether the compounding is sustained is precisely what is unknown.

The two regimes can be stated as marginal cost curves. On Earth, the marginal cost of the n-th node can rise as the operator bids up land, congests grids, and encounters political and thermal limits. In space, after closure, the marginal cost can fall through learning and self-replication. One curve rises and the other falls; their crossover is the migration point, and it moves earlier as launch cost declines, closure improves, equipment life lengthens, or qualification premiums fall. Part II shows that the curves do not cross at the anchored bridge-economy values.

Model check. The cost-curve claim — Earth’s marginal node rises with n, space’s falls with n after closure — is the crossover surface, and at anchored values the curves do not cross. The scenario needs three demanding unanchored conditions: rad-tolerance at commodity cost (the strongest current data supports five-year TID survivability but leaves system reliability — SEE, training workloads, thermal, whole-spacecraft — unresolved [S32]), service life nearer 15 years than 5, and target-class launch or closure substituting for launch. The collector-area arithmetic is not the disputed part; the three demanding unanchored conditions are where the scenario lives.

Two conditions attach. Demand saturation: if the set of tasks worth computing is bounded, demand saturates and the argument that space is the only arena permitting unbounded deployment loses its motivation [S34]. The physical ceilings bound how cheaply computation can be done; a demand ceiling would bound how much is wanted — the more decisive and less examined of the two. The non-saturation branch has a canonical published statement [S35] and no resolution; the scenario is conditional on it. The upgrade asymmetry, narrowed: software-layer improvements propagate to deployed compute at near-zero marginal cost, but hardware-dependent gains require replacement or retrofit — silicon is not upgraded in place. The model consequence: the space-electronics obsolescence term would shrink after convergence only for its software-limited share.

IV.3 Paradigm shifts: delay, alteration, or prevention

Catch-up time (a new paradigm must beat the incumbent plus decades of compounded process learning, still improving as the newcomer matures) and finiteness (irreversible-computation paradigms climb toward the same ceiling; reversible computing is the stated exception) bound the leapfrog objection. Exposure is concentrated in fabrication on 10–20-year horizons; energy, labor, transport, and materials are less paradigm-sensitive — substantially reusable, not immune. The fleet self-insures through its own 3–6-year depreciation; the fab carries the stranding risk — the penalty of taking the lead.

General-purpose robotic manufacturing is a partial hedge because it is the industry that builds industries: after a paradigm shift, the cheapest retrofitter may be the actor able to build the next fab faster than a rival builds its first. The corresponding strategy is to verticalize the less paradigm-sensitive layers aggressively, preserve hardware generality and retooling capacity at the paradigm-specific layer, and track retooling speed alongside doubling time. The model check below shows that this hedge must be pre-positioned; it cannot be improvised after a catastrophic electronics loss.

Model check. The paradigm-sensitivity split maps onto the model’s sector structure: a shift perturbs the electronics column of the requirement matrix and the fab layer behind the vitamin imports — exactly the sector already identified as binding in the relevant architectures. Machine tools and robotics are necessary retooling capabilities, but all eight modeled physical production sectors are knockout-indispensable; the knockout experiment does not show that those two are uniquely more strategically valuable. Retooling speed is a computed output (cutsets.retooling_time), and it hardens this scenario’s central risk into a result: destroying 90% of the electronics or machine-tools sector at any point on the central trajectory is model-fatal — a defined, horizon-relative label: worst-case growth has not returned positive within the tested 20-year post-knockout window while the unknocked counterfactual’s stays positive, under both the myopic and receding-horizon allocators, and at optimistic values too. The computation tests a 20-year horizon under the stated deterministic configuration; it establishes no recovery within that window, not permanent impossibility — a longer horizon, resumed imports, altered plant design, larger initial surplus, or a lower knock fraction could change the outcome and are unswept. The mechanism is the electronics strategic-material gap: at electronics q-scale 0.10–0.30, replacement local capacity is a multi-decade-payback asset no plausible planning horizon rebuilds from current output. Only power stranding under optimistic values is a finite delay (~27 years lost). Conditional implication: within this scenario class, a paradigm shift that obsoletes the local electronics tier removes the self-expansion margin for at least a two-decade window unless Earth imports resume — so the leapfrog hedge must be pre-positioned (hardware generality, retooling-ready lines, retained umbilical capacity), because post-shift rebuild from inside the complex is not a path the model offers within any tested horizon. Caveats: deterministic values, 90% single-sector knockout, maximin allocation family, 20-year window; surplus-pinning (stage 3), knock-fraction sweeps, and longer-horizon recovery tests remain open follow-ups.

IV.4 The alternative telos, and the properly conditional close

One reading of the same physics reaches this document’s destination from opposite values: Earth is not a constrained platform to escape but a uniquely valuable biosphere to protect — zone the planet for habitation, site heavy industry and compute where there is no ecology to disturb [S34]. Independent corroboration of the operating-wall mechanism comes from the same quarter: data-center siting is politically contested over electricity, water, and land. The physical argument is common to both readings; only the telos differs — and this decouples P3 from P4: the migration case can be made without any claim about one company’s intentions.

The observed portfolio is consistent with an economic gradient toward greater integration — discovery until convergence, deployment after it, with space as one plausible arena under a demanding set of crossover conditions that this analysis has now priced. Present evidence does not establish that recursive off-world industrial closure is the governing objective of the companies described in Part III. The initial argument said a model could decide; the repository now executes that model. What the model says is: the recursion is feasible only under assumptions that are currently choices rather than measurements; the economics point to Earth at every anchored value; and the observations that would change either conclusion are now named, ranked, and waiting.

Limitations and claim boundary

The most robust outputs are structural within the implemented model: balanced doubling is unit-invariant; the three-stage allocator has a unique state transition; realized endpoints include same-step shocks; recoverable scrap cannot exceed loss-specific retirement; and Part II is exactly affine in launch price. Architecture comparisons, endpoint definitions, and regeneration from fixed seeds are also auditable.

The substantive conclusions remain assumption-conditioned. In the inherited model, the requirement matrix, homogeneous electronics-closure multiplier, repair and recovery efficiencies, stockpiles, shock process, import profile, and finite capture reservoir are not measured as a coupled industrial system. Its scalar-anchor screen does not rank structural matrix uncertainty, interactions, policy families, or all environments, and its LEO model has neither an endogenous debris stock nor a depleted capture reservoir.

The integrated layer adds a material-category-by-sector bill of materials, source yields, Earth–Moon–orbit–asteroid transfer arcs, seed-mass and composition-changing Pareto searches, a decomposed knowledge package, observable autonomy gates, process-specific environment profiles, construction and transport lags, cohort-resolved commissioning and yield ramps, architecture-specific viable floors, independent sector allocation, explicit repair, finite orbital feed, and shell-resolved debris. A separate delivery diagnostic distinguishes delivered, staged, installed, commissioned, failed, recovered, and operating seed states. These are model features, not validated factories. Their bills of material, recoverable yields, source throughput, autonomy/productivity gains, lag/ramp/repair coefficients, intervention budget, source portfolio, transfer capacities, environment responses, and collision kernels are declared assumptions. The seed is minimum-mass only inside the enumerated architecture and design alternatives. Seventeen material categories do not resolve mineralogy, alloying routes, contamination, process chemistry, purity ladders, tool wear, quality yield, or every consumable. The electronics tiers remain aggregates rather than fabs and tool chains. Documented elemental occurrence is not a grade distribution, recoverable reserve, refining yield, or accessible asteroid portfolio. The process-closure acceptance contract in params/process_closure_requirements.yaml makes the missing graph explicit: source lots, species, unit processes, grades, critical parts, parent tools, transport legs, waste routes, evidence records, and eight binary gates. The generated process_closure_gap_register.csv remains wholly evidence_pending; the contract does not itself supply those nodes or data. The associated bundle evaluator rejects graphs that omit a grade, critical part family, process stage, evidence hash, or independently witnessed gate.

The terrestrial rehearsal in I.9 remains a proposed validation protocol, not an accomplished demonstration; its computed scenario is a requirements case, not an experiment. Its machine-validated event and acceptance contract is published in params/rehearsal_protocol.yaml, with the unexecuted public matrix in outputs/integrated/tables/rehearsal_acceptance_matrix.csv. The evidence-bundle evaluator likewise refuses a result unless every event type and injected fault, archive and auditor hash, witnessed gate, and parameter-replacement record is present. Environment profiles now change throughput, yield, power, depreciation, and binding rows, but their multipliers do not simulate granular mechanics, convection, melt behavior, vacuum welding, abrasive dust, radiation damage, traction, or thermal-cycle physics. The compute–intelligence loop remains phenomenological even though its gates are expressed as observable task completion, intervention, diagnosis, verification, engineering-cycle, yield, repair-success, and recovery quantities. The shell model is a stress model, not a conjunction-assessment or validated traffic simulation.

Part II now includes communications and ground-network capex, spacecraft-bus functions, program NRE, insurance, spectrum/regulatory cost, disposal, residual value, thermal margins, workload boundaries, and separate financing. Serviceability remains a scenario rather than an observed property. A symmetric dynamic economics diagnostic couples technical space capacity and its construction, transfer, and intervention demand to the same investment, financing, learning, depreciation, regulatory-delay, and market mechanics used for Earth. Its coefficients are assumption-class and neither tested space case self-finances inside 40 years, so P3b remains unresolved rather than inferred from physical compounding. The claim-level provenance audit reclassified inherited reporting-derived Part II intervals as ASSUMPTION wherever no source directly supported the modeled endpoints and transformation. Every remaining non-ASSUMPTION anchor now resolves through params/claim_provenance.yaml to an exact locator, extracted value, units, transformation, and persistent identifier; the generated public table is outputs/tables/claim_provenance.csv. This makes the evidence boundary auditable, but it does not empirically calibrate the wide assumption ranges. The r4.0 economic-calibration contract in params/economic_calibration.yaml defines architecture-specific evidence, equal-workload fields, correlated fitting groups, audited dated cash flows, chronological holdout validation, and the promotion rule. Its public readiness table is entirely data_pending; P3b remains empirically open. Its bundle evaluator requires all evidence packages, correlated fits, holdouts, cash-flow event types, immutable hashes, and reviewed parameter decisions; point estimates alone cannot satisfy it. Finally, the Part III strategy assessment is ordinal and observational: corporate filings and statements establish declared initiatives, not an intent to achieve recursive closure. No result in this paper is a forecast or an empirical probability of success.

A.7 Provisional hiring-sweep note — not an evidence-table item

A July 2026 search across 1,170 open OpenAI and Anthropic postings found multiple roles explicitly concerned with software-RSI preparation and measurement, including early-warning metrics, recursive-self-improvement preparation, chip-design reinforcement learning, and long-horizon training environments. The same search found no roles in fabrication, packaging/test, materials, or production-equipment reproduction. This is a provisional negative-search observation, not evidence of capability or a model input. Its value depends on the unpublished search vocabulary, deduplication rules, per-lab counts, and stability of a changing jobs corpus. The working snapshot is docs/transcripts/lab-job-listings-2026-07-26.md; it should not enter the main evidence table until a public dated audit artifact exists.

Appendix B: Implementation and Provenance

The executable release combines the ten-sector capacity model, the comparative economics model, and an 18-sector, 17-material integrated-bootstrap layer. The integrated layer includes material-category-resolved bills of material, explicit source and transfer arcs, minimum-mass seed sizing, autonomy and intervention constraints, process-environment effects, construction and commissioning dynamics, compute–intelligence–productivity coupling, tiered electronics, finite shell mass, debris dynamics, symmetric economics, and composition-changing robust-seed searches.

Central and 200-draw deterministic assumption-ensemble results are reported in Part I.8 and regenerate from scripts/run_integrated.py. The release includes sector-resolved cohort dynamics, independent allocation and repair, delivered- seed deployment, observable autonomy and outage regimes, policy and structural sweeps, terminal-window diagnostics, import-stock resolution, coupling ablations, an oversize frontier, and a quantified strict-lunar infeasibility certificate. All remain assumption-conditioned structures pending empirical calibration.

Machine-validated contracts define the still-missing evidence for process-feasible closure, the physical Stage-0 rehearsal, and economic calibration. Their templates are deliberately non-passing: completed bundles must bind every referenced digest to a verified file, and success states must satisfy the underlying fault, holdout, review, and graph-consistency rules. Venue-specific paper drafts and submission contracts are included, but final source/style review, live-portal checks, author-controlled declarations, immutable release coordinates, and submission approval remain pending.

Every generated result is reproducible from the declared configuration, code, and deterministic seeds. outputs/MANIFEST.md binds the canonical manuscript, HTML, source/configuration files, and generated artifacts; outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md additionally records the integrated run inputs and outputs. No model output is presented as a measurement, empirical probability, engineering estimate, or forecast.

Model: src/rsimodel/{model,delta,cutsets,montecarlo,lco,policies,plots,report}.py; parameters: params/{anchors,assumptions,environments}.yaml; generated reports with per-run provenance tables and machine-readable CSV summaries: outputs/ (headline table: outputs/tables/mc_deep.csv). Stages 1–2 of each allocation use HiGHS through a persistent warm-started model, with scipy.optimize.linprog as the retained reference/fallback path and RSI_SLOW_LP=1 to force it. Stage 3 uses the pinned OSQP solver for the strictly convex normalized tie-breaker, with a numerical fallback. All randomness flows through explicitly seeded numpy.random.Generator instances; every script derives its seeds from stable crc32 strings (never Python’s process-salted hash()), and each anchor’s Monte Carlo draw is keyed by the run seed plus the anchor’s NAME, so results are stable both across processes and under anchor-list growth. All tables regenerate deterministically within a pinned reference environment. outputs/MANIFEST.md records the sha256 of every release artifact, including the canonical Markdown and standalone HTML, plus library versions; it omits a self-referential generating-commit field. tests/test_repro.py cross-checks the committed CSV against the committed report so mutually stale artifacts fail the suite. outputs/report_deep.md and outputs/tables/mc_deep.csv are written by a single execution of one script and cannot diverge. Structural coefficients are ASSUMPTION-class and live only inside named assumption sets.

The integrated model is src/rsimodel/integrated.py, with the r4.0 analysis module in src/rsimodel/integrated_analysis.py, configured entirely by params/integrated_model.yaml and run by scripts/run_integrated.py. outputs/integrated/report.md, 33 CSV tables, and five figures are generated from one in-memory scenario set. outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md records the sha256 of the configuration, implementation, runner, focused tests, and every generated artifact. Its ensemble uses 200 deterministic named draws per scenario from seed 404. Adding a draw or changing a coefficient changes the manifest; none of that upgrades an assumption to evidence.

Appendix D: Complete model specification

Everything a reader needs to reconstruct the Part I model without opening the implementation. Part II’s cost model is fully specified by its affine form (II.2) plus the anchor table (A.4), with two implementation details: the annualization applies component-specific lives (compute hardware and its replacement launch mass on compute.life_years_space; PV, radiator, storage, structure, and their launch spend on power_systems.infrastructure_life_years, floored at the hardware life — the LCO remains exactly affine in launch $/kg), and each Monte Carlo iteration resolves every anchor once per cached AnchorSet so Earth and space share common physical draws while retaining separate financing anchors. This appendix covers the multisector dynamics and then specifies the paper layer that runs beside it.

D.1 Integrated-bootstrap layer

State space. The implementation has 18 sectors: power, mining, refining, robotics, machine tools, construction, thermal, transport, repair, recycling, interconnects/boards, passives/power, sensors/control, packaging/test, mature logic, advanced logic/memory, process equipment/metrology, and compute. It tracks 17 material categories: O, Si, Al, Fe, Mg, Ca, Ti, H, C, N, Cu, Ni, Co, Cr, Li, rare earths, and dopants — 15 elements plus two material classes, so the model is material-category-resolved rather than element-resolved: stoichiometric and process-chemical closure is not checked at the species level. The full coefficient set is the machine-readable specification in params/integrated_model.yaml.

Material and service closure. For material category ee, sector jj, and source/transfer arc aa:

ΔMe=∑sYs,eXs+Ie+∑aFa,ein−∑jBe,jxj−Le−∑aFa,eout, \Delta M_e = \sum_s Y_{s,e}X_s + I_e + \sum_a F^{\mathrm{in}}_{a,e} - \sum_j B_{e,j}x_j - L_e - \sum_a F^{\mathrm{out}}_{a,e},

where Be,jB_{e,j} is the amount of material category ee required per unit of sector-jj build, Ys,eY_{s,e} is the recoverable yield from source and process ss, and Fa,eF_{a,e} is material flow across an Earth, lunar surface, orbital, or asteroid transfer arc. Concentration alone does not set YY; mineral form, beneficiation, refining energy, purity, and loss remain outside the occurrence citations. Service closure uses Ai,jA_{i,j}, the sector-ii service output needed to build and replace sector jj. Recoverable lunar and asteroid yields, rather than bulk inventory, enter the constraints. Earth material appears only as the bounded initial strategic-material import stock vev_e.

Process environment and autonomy. For each process jj, task coverage at AI level II is

cj(I)=min⁡{cjmax,cj0+αjmax⁡(I−1,0)}. c_j(I)=\min\{c_j^{\max},\ c_j^0+\alpha_j\max(I-1,0)\}.

Effective productivity is multiplied by (0.5+0.5cj)(0.5+0.5c_j) — a declared ASSUMPTION-class convention assigning fully scripted, conventionally automated operation half of full productivity at zero unscripted-task coverage, not a measured relation. Residual annual intervention is hj(1−cj)zjh_j(1-c_j)z_j and its sum must fit the scenario budget; the linear form treats missing autonomy as smoothly divisible labor demand and does not represent threshold effects, where one unrecoverable diagnosis, calibration, or repair task stops a line despite high average coverage. Where declared required acceleration gj*g_j^\ast exceeds lunar gravity gL=0.165gg_L=0.165g, the acceleration gap adds centrifuge structural material and parasitic power. The reported centrifuge speed follows

rpmj=602π9.80665max⁡(gj*−gL,0)rj. \mathrm{rpm}_j=\frac{60}{2\pi} \sqrt{\frac{9.80665\max(g_j^\ast-g_L,0)}{r_j}}.

This is an equipment penalty, not a claim that a whole lunar factory or habitat requires artificial gravity.

Seed sizing. Decision variables are sector capacities zjz_j, annual lunar and asteroid feed pL,pAp_L,p_A, and initial Earth strategic-material stocks vev_e. The linear program minimizes

Mseed=Mdigital+∑jzj∑eBe,jeff+∑eve, M_{\mathrm{seed}} = M_{\mathrm{digital}}+\sum_j z_j\sum_e B_{e,j}^{\mathrm{eff}} +\sum_e v_e,

subject to minimum viable sector capacities, task coverage and intervention limits, service output sufficient for replacement plus one complete second cell, element balances through each scenario horizon, and mining, refining, transport, and energy throughput. Sector commissioning lags and half-ramp loss reduce productive years. Mdigital=5M_{\mathrm{digital}}=5 t represents the software, simulation, industrial-memory, and experimental package; its value is an assumption, not a storage-mass estimate.

The LP can also minimize Earth-import mass or intervention demand, using installed mass as a lexicographic secondary objective. All three objectives return the same central design in every LP-feasible scenario. This is not a Pareto frontier: it shows that the present variables contain no alternative process or redundancy choices capable of trading those objectives.

Dynamic sector-capacity growth. A feasible seed begins as one installed and operating cell — delivery, unloading, site preparation, and first commissioning are outside the model, so seed mass refers to an installed operating nucleus, not a self-deploying delivered package. Each quarter, lunar production, commissioned asteroid production, and recovered retirement enter inventory. New orders use the complete balanced sector-and-material vector of the seed design. For each sector jj, installed capacity KjK_j, operating capacity OjO_j, ordered capacity, its declared commissioning lag, yield ramp, and depreciation δj\delta_j remain stateful. Retired material is recovered by category at the declared 82% fraction. Lunar feed scales with operating mining, refining, and power; asteroid feed additionally requires operating transport. An incomplete packet contributes only the output qjOjq_jO_j of sectors already operating. The reported cell-equivalent aggregate is derived as min⁡jOj/zj\min_j O_j/z_j, and the doubling threshold is first passage of that minimum to 2.0. It is not the discrete commissioning of a second factory’s subsystems and not, by itself, evidence of sustained growth. Balanced packets remain a restriction: the dynamic allocator cannot yet choose an independent sector composition or explicit repair action.

Installed compute CtC_t raises normalized intelligence according to

It+Δt=min⁡{Imax,It+ℓvlog⁡(1+Ct/C0)Δt}, I_{t+\Delta t} = \min\{I_{\max}, I_t +\ell\,v\log(1+C_t/C_0)\Delta t\},

where ℓ\ell is the learning coefficient and vv the verification factor. Intelligence above the scenario starting level raises both industrial productivity and autonomy, which raises cell output and future compute. Earth and Earth-fed orbital counterfactuals instead add capacity at constant, scenario-specific build/delivery rates, subtract 0.16/yr depreciation, and impose terrestrial site ceilings. Moon→orbit compute has a 0.5-year lag, a 35% share of new endogenous capacity, and a transport-capacity ceiling.

Debris state. A separate stress test evolves active assets, derelicts, and a fragment index. Failures, controlled disposal, retrieval, collisions, fragment creation, natural clearance, and active removal are explicit. RdebrisR_{\mathrm{debris}} — the five-year fragment creation-to-clearance ratio — is fragments created divided by fragments cleared over the last five years: a flow ratio, not a branching-process reproduction number. Realized clearance is capped by the fragments available, so at an empty fragment stock the ratio reads exactly one. The distributed case multiplies the collision kernel by 0.01; it is therefore a declared topology test, not a derived property of heliocentric space.

Scenarios and uncertainty. The four named cases are terrestrial rehearsal, lunar strategic-material bridge, strict lunar-only, and Moon–asteroid network. Their horizons, AI levels, import caps, intervention budgets, and source commissioning dates are all explicit in the YAML. Each 200-run ensemble uses stable crc32 names from seed 404 to draw independent log-uniform multipliers for service productivity, bills of material, lunar and asteroid yield, depreciation, lag, and autonomy gap. Frequencies across those draws are design-space occupancy, not empirical probabilities. Tests verify dimensions, nonnegative balances, strict-lunar infeasibility, finite-import-stock behavior, gravity overhead, aggregate-capacity doubling, named-draw stability, and the debris threshold. outputs/integrated/MANIFEST.md binds the configuration, implementation, runner, tests, tables, figures, and report.

r4.0 analysis module. src/rsimodel/integrated_analysis.py adds derived diagnostics over the same declared coefficients, inventing none: terminal-window endpoints (retention at horizon, final-five-year net capacity change, import-pool exhaustion timing); strategic-import-stock resolution; zero/freeze intelligence-coupling ablations; the installed-mass-versus-aggregate-doubling oversize frontier (simulate_capacity_growth(initial_cells=f) installs f cell-equivalents of the fixed minimum-mass design); per-draw ensemble diagnostics over the identical named crc32 draws (failure reasons, binding-constraint frequencies, Spearman sensitivity); and an elastic-relaxation infeasibility certificate that interrogates the exact seed LP through a shared matrix builder. The expanded module also compares independent allocation and explicit repair, observable knowledge/autonomy outages, process-environment profiles, finite-mass shell debris, policy and structural-shock sweeps, shelf-limited electronics architectures, symmetric dynamic economics, and composition-changing robust-seed Pareto designs. Twenty-nine tables and five figures regenerate with the run, including the full sector trajectory and an 80-year central extension. These diagnostics add structure and falsification plumbing; their coefficients remain assumptions pending empirical calibration.

D.2 Inherited ten-sector model

Sectors and units. n = 10 sectors, ordered: power, mining, refining, robotics, machine_tools, electronics, thermal, transport, repair, recycling. Capacity K_j is in abstract capacity units (K_j(0) = 1 for all j unless stated); sector j produces q_j output units per capacity unit per year (q below is the central set after environment q-scaling for the lunar architecture is applied via environments.yaml; the tabulated q is the pre-scaling set value). Repair and recycling are service sectors: their rows in A are zero, and their outputs are consumed as described below.

Time. Discrete steps of Δt = 0.25 yr (0.5 yr for cut-set enumeration), default horizon 35–40 yr. This inherited layer has no construction lags, commissioning delays, yield ramps, or minimum efficient scales — all its outputs are stylized model outputs, not engineering timescale forecasts.

Imports. m_i(t) = B₀ · e^(−t/τ) · φ_i, with per-sector cutoffs (m_i := 0 for i in the cut set after the cutoff year). Stockable sectors’ imports flow into the stockpile; non-stockable flow into the current balance. Mars: stockable imports arrive as synodic batches of size m·(2.14 yr) every 2.14 yr.

Allocation (per step): three-stage lexicographic optimization. Variables: builds x ∈ ℝⁿ₊, wear-repair u ∈ ℝⁿ₊, recycling activity w ∈ ℝ₊, stockpile drawdown d ∈ ℝⁿ₊ (d_i = 0 for non-stockable i), growth floor g ∈ ℝ.

Stage 1 — maximize g subject to:

xj+uj−δjKj≥gKj∀j,uj≤δwear,jKj∀j,∑jAijxj+sf∑jAijuj+𝟏i=repair1ηrep∑juj+𝟏i=recyclingw+oiw−ρiw−di≤qiKi+mdirect,i∀i,w+ηscrap∑jfwear,juj≤ηscrap∑j,cfc,jδc,jKj,di≤SiΔt. \begin{aligned} x_j + u_j - \delta_j K_j &\ge gK_j && \forall j, \\ u_j &\le \delta_{\mathrm{wear},j}K_j && \forall j, \\ \sum_j A_{ij}x_j + s_f\sum_j A_{ij}u_j + \mathbf{1}_{i=\mathrm{repair}}\frac{1}{\eta_{\mathrm{rep}}}\sum_j u_j + \mathbf{1}_{i=\mathrm{recycling}}w + o_iw-\rho_iw-d_i &\le q_iK_i+m_{\mathrm{direct},i} && \forall i, \\ w+\eta_{\mathrm{scrap}}\sum_j f_{\mathrm{wear},j}u_j &\le \eta_{\mathrm{scrap}} \sum_{j,c}f_{c,j}\delta_{c,j}K_j, \\ d_i &\le \frac{S_i}{\Delta t}. \end{aligned}

with s_f = spares fraction (0.15), η_rep = repair efficiency (0.75 central), η_scrap = processing yield (0.40 central, < 1 always), o = recycling opex vector, ρ = recycling output profile, and f_c,j = the recoverable share of loss component c in sector j. Equivalently, available retirement before processing is

R(K,u)=∑j,cfc,jδc,jKj−∑jfwear,juj. R(K,u)=\sum_{j,c}f_{c,j}\delta_{c,j}K_j -\sum_j f_{\mathrm{wear},j}u_j.

The environment defaults are:

environment wear catastrophic obsolescence logistics
LEO 1.00 0.00 1.00 0.00
lunar 1.00 0.50 1.00 0.00
Mars 1.00 0.25 1.00 0.00
Earth 1.00 0.80 1.00 0.00

Stage 2 holds g at its optimum and minimizes dimensionless stock draw ∑iωidi\sum_i\omega_i d_i, where ωi\omega_i is the inverse of a same-unit scale based on current supply and available stock, normalized by the largest weight. Stock is a buffer, not fuel, and the objective is invariant to changes in sector row units.

Stage 3 holds the stage-1 and stage-2 optima within solver tolerance and minimizes a strictly convex normalized action norm:

min⁡[∑jxj2+uj2K̂j2+w2R̂2+∑idi2D̂i2+g2]. \min\left[ \sum_j\frac{x_j^2+u_j^2}{\widehat K_j^2} +\frac{w^2}{\widehat R^2} +\sum_i\frac{d_i^2}{\widehat D_i^2} +g^2\right].

All scales are positive state-derived quantities with numerical floors. The positive-definite Hessian makes the selected action, and therefore the state transition, unique. Stage 1 and 2 use HiGHS; stage 3 uses OSQP with a public SLSQP fallback for rare narrow-face numerical failures.

State updates and shocks.

Kj←max⁡(Kj+Δt(xj+uj−δjKj),10−9),Si←clip⁡(Si+inflowi−diΔt−SiΔtLi,0,Ci). \begin{aligned} K_j &\leftarrow \max\!\left(K_j+\Delta t\,(x_j+u_j-\delta_jK_j),10^{-9}\right), \\ S_i &\leftarrow \operatorname{clip}\!\left( S_i+\mathrm{inflow}_i-d_i\Delta t-\frac{S_i\Delta t}{L_i}, 0,C_i \right). \end{aligned}

with shelf life L_i (electronics 5 yr central), capacity cap C_i = c_years · Σ_j A[i,j] δ_j K_j (replacement demand), initial stock S_i(0) = s_years · replacement demand at t = 0, stockable sectors only (robotics, machine tools, electronics, repair). Common-cause shocks are applied after this deterministic capacity update; the stock cap is then recomputed from the damaged capacity. Reported timestamps and shock-log timestamps are the step end t+Δtt+\Delta t. The headline realized growth is

greal=minjKj,postshock−Kj,prestepΔtKj,prestep, g_{\mathrm{real}}= \min_j\frac{K_{j,\mathrm{postshock}}-K_{j,\mathrm{prestep}}} {\Delta t\,K_{j,\mathrm{prestep}}},

while the allocator’s pre-shock g*g^* is retained separately as g_alloc.

Depreciation. δ_j = δ_wear,j + δ_catastrophic,j + δ_obsolescence,j + δ_logistics,j per environment (environments.yaml), anchored entries resolved at geometric mids (deterministic) or loguniform draws (MC), one shared draw per anchor per run. Obsolescence is included on the reading that K is frontier-equivalent capacity (A.1’s five-quantity separation).

Shocks. Per step and per shock class: N ~ Poisson(rate · Δt) events; each multiplies K over its sector group by (1 − f), f ~ U(f_lo, f_hi). Rates jittered ±30% per MC run (ASSUMPTION).

Outcome definitions. Expanding at year 30: realized post-shock g > 0 at the step ending at year 30 — the instantaneous, weakest endpoint; it does not preclude import- or stock-supported growth or near-zero absolute capacity (a minimum-viable-scale criterion needs an authorial threshold and is queued). The pre-shock allocation endpoint uses g_alloc and is diagnostic only. Sustained: realized g > 0 at every recorded step ending in years 25–30. Earth-import cutoff: a separate central-set ensemble with all Earth imports cut at year 30; the endpoint is realized g > 0 throughout 30–35 (stock draw permitted). LEO retains capture feed and is labeled accordingly, not as autonomy. Balanced doubling (headline replication metric): first t with λ(t) = min_j K_j(t)/K_j(0) ≥ 2 — unit-invariant, requires every sector to double in its own capacity units; it is not a claim that a complete second physical seed has been commissioned. Aggregate doubling (continuity diagnostic): first t with Σ_j K_j(t) ≥ 2 Σ_j K_j(0), measured against the supplied K(0) — unit-dependent, reported alongside but never as “system replication”. Both doubling metrics are reported over all runs that ever reach the criterion and conditioned on year-30 survivors — the difference is the doubled-then-failed class.

Binding sector and co-binding. At each allocation step, each material-balance supply is relaxed by 1% and stage 1 is re-solved. The finite response Δgi\Delta g_i is unit-invariant because both the perturbation and row quantity scale together. Every positive response within 5% of the largest forms the co-binding set and shares fractional credit. If all responses are numerically zero, relative slack supplies a display fallback only. The baseline and allocation-policy comparison use the same definition.

Central-set structural coefficients (ASSUMPTION-class; conservative = central with A×1.35, δ×1.4, τ=10 yr, and reduced repair/recycling/stock scales; optimistic = A×0.75, δ×0.8, τ=25 yr, increased scales; full machine-readable sets in params/assumptions.yaml):

Glossary

Recursive self-improvement (RSI): a process in which an intelligent system contributes to producing a more capable successor.

Industrial closure (κ): the degree to which a production network internally supplies the critical inputs required for its own operation. The proper object is a sector vector with criticality and substitutability, not a single mass fraction.

Closure engineering: the quantitative discipline, originating in the 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study, of accounting for every input a replicating industrial system must produce or import.

Self-sustaining: able to replace consumed and depreciated productive capacity without an essential external supply.

Self-expanding: able to produce net additional productive capacity after replacement, repair, and losses.

Industrial seed: a compact initial system intended to grow into a broader local production network. In this paper it has four layers: physical equipment; digital models and toolchains; industrial memory; and experimental capacity for generating missing knowledge.

Digital seed: the AI weights, firmware, controllers, compilers, CAD/CAM, simulators, optimization and verification tools, and locally available software dependencies transported with an industrial seed.

Industrial memory: the machine-readable recipes, material and equipment models, calibration and maintenance procedures, build records, failure histories, intervention traces, and provenance required to operate, repair, and adapt the physical seed.

Embodied-autonomy threshold: the task coverage and recovery capability at which a robot-and-AI system can perform the unscripted diagnosis, tool use, construction, repair, learning, and verification needed to keep the industrial graph operating without routine human intervention. It is not a joint-count or robot-count threshold.

Terrestrial autonomous-closure rehearsal: an Earth-based test of the candidate off-world seed under constrained materials, energy, communications, spares, and human access, culminating in construction and commissioning of a second production cell.

Operating-cell equivalent: the integrated layer’s continuous unit of installed, commissioned productive capacity, normalized to the initial seed cell. The reported aggregate-doubling threshold is first passage of this aggregate to 2.0; it is not a claim that a discrete second factory has completed commissioning or that expansion is sustained.

Exogenous deployment: capacity growth supplied by an external industrial base, such as Earth-manufactured data centers delivered to orbit.

Endogenous industrial growth: capacity growth produced from within the industrial network by allocating part of its output to reproducing and expanding productive equipment.

Material vitamins: low-mass, high-criticality inputs—such as advanced chips, dopants, catalysts, specialty chemicals, sensors, bearings, or precision tooling—whose absence can stop a high-mass locally supplied industry.

Process-specific artificial gravity: centrifugal acceleration supplied to a particular machine or production module when microgravity or lunar gravity does not meet that process’s requirements; distinct from rotating an entire habitat or industrial complex.

Clock-setting component: the component with the shortest effective replacement horizon that cannot yet be produced, repaired, substituted, or stockpiled locally; it bounds the survival time of the partially closed system.

Replication time: the time a production network needs to reproduce a unit of productive capacity. It is unknown as a measurement here and appears only as a set-labeled model-output distribution.

Bridge economy: the sequence of independently financeable products and services that carries the system through the capital-intensive stages before closure.

ISRU: in-situ resource utilization — obtaining and using materials at the mission destination rather than importing every supply from Earth.

Productive throughput: the rate at which a system converts energy, materials, compute, and machine time into useful output.

Distributed industrial ecology: a network of specialized, mutually dependent production nodes whose combined input-output graph is self-sustaining or self-expanding.

Scarcity becomes latency: the proposition that, after high closure, the principal limit on many outputs becomes production allocation and completion time rather than external purchase price. Opportunity cost remains.

Von Neumann replicator: a machine system capable of constructing a functional copy of itself from available materials; the formal category to which a fully closed industrial complex belongs.

Terafab: the chip-fabrication initiative announced in March 2026 by Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI and joined by Intel in April, targeting advanced AI chips including radiation-tolerant orbital silicon. The SEC-filed offering materials describe a general framework with unsettled implementation, not a demonstrated fab or legally constituted joint venture [S27].

Society-priced costs: operating inputs priced substantially through human institutions rather than physical conversion alone — land, permitting, interconnection, litigation, and political consent. Space relocates these costs toward gateways such as launch, spectrum, liability, and treaty rather than abolishing them.

Threshold-model argument: the proposition that once a base model crosses the capability needed to run verified improvement loops, a smarter starting model may confer only a transient head start and durable advantage may shift toward hardware doubling time and industrial closure. This is the small-α branch of II.5, not an established law.

Architectural convergence: the point at which the marginal value of another design improvement falls below that of another deployed node. Beyond it, growth is increasingly deployment-limited.

Paradigm-sensitivity split: the division between less paradigm-sensitive layers — energy, labor, transport, and bulk materials — and the more paradigm-specific fabrication layer, where stranding and leapfrog risk concentrate.

Retooling speed: the time a manufacturing complex needs to reconfigure for a new technological paradigm. Alongside hardware doubling time, it is a first-class competitive and resilience metric.

Physical-process data: training-relevant data generated by operating physical industry — telemetry, process settings, intervention records, failures, and fleet or manipulation traces.

Data-advantage index (κ_D): an index over uniqueness, causal linkage, coverage, quality, accessibility, integration, and verification value. Total training-relevant data has no measurable denominator, so κ_D is not a closure ratio.

Unified build record: a per-unit data structure linking design intent (as designed), production parameters (as built), and operational telemetry (as deployed), making physical-process data causally trainable.

Vitamin parts (historical term): the residual imported microelectronics, bearings, precision instruments, catalysts, or other high-complexity inputs that resist local production. The term comes from the 1980 closure literature.

Electronics strategic-material gap: in this model, the unclosable fraction of the electronics sector’s output mix — the results-driving unknown sampled through the space electronics q-scale. It is also called the “vitamin gap” in the closure literature.

Coasean boundary: the organizational boundary at which internal coordination costs equal market transaction costs. AI can lower both sides, so the direction in which the efficient boundary moves is empirical.

Gateway leverage: enforceable governance authority concentrated at dependencies such as launch, spectrum, export control, finance, communications, cryptographic authority, and trade. Its material component follows criticality, substitutability, stockpile, supplier concentration, and enforceability — not the scalar expression (1 − κ).

Minimum cut set: a smallest combination of imported inputs whose loss prevents self-expansion.

Likelihood ratio of evidence: how much more expected an observation is under one hypothesis than under a competitor. Part III uses ordinal diagnosticity rather than numerical multiplication because evidence items are correlated and observability is uncertain.

Maximin growth rate g: the worst-case sector growth rate maximized by the allocation program, ensuring that aggregate growth cannot hide collapse in an indispensable sector.

Assumption set: a named, complete collection of ASSUMPTION-class structural coefficients used together in a model run.

Anchor: a published, source-classed range sampled by Monte Carlo; an anchor constrains an input without converting it into a measurement of the whole system.

Computed: derived mechanically from stated assumptions by the companion model. A computed result inherits the epistemic class of its weakest input.

Kessler syndrome / collisional cascade: an endogenous orbital-debris feedback in which collisions create fragments that increase the probability of later collisions. It is not equivalent to a fixed independent debris hazard.

Sun-synchronous orbit (SSO): a planet-centered precessing orbit selected so that the spacecraft passes a reference point at approximately the same local solar time. Earth SSO is ordinarily a LEO architecture; it does not mean an orbit around the Sun.

Heliocentric orbit: an orbit around the Sun. In the post-lunar scenario, “distributed heliocentric” means separated orbital elements and resource trajectories rather than a new single dense shell.

Sources [S1–S27] establish the core argument and [S28] identifies the executed companion model. [S29–S36] add corporate, technical, and fast-takeoff/capital-mobilization cross-checks. [S37] is the primary June 2026 Starship V3/V4 disclosure used to normalize the launch-price sensitivity cases; [S38] is the subsequent AI1 product specification. [S39–S44] are the independent spacecraft, thermal, network, microdatacenter, and economic cross-checks added to Part II in the post-IPO calibration pass.

SpaceX states that establishing a self-sufficient city on Mars requires large-scale cargo and population transfer.

[S2] Tesla, “Master Plan Part 3”.

Tesla outlines a proposed path to a sustainable global energy economy through electrification, renewable generation, and storage.

[S3] xAI, “Company: Accelerating Scientific Discovery”.

xAI describes its mission as accelerating scientific discovery and extending what humanity can know and do.

NASA describes technologies for using destination resources to produce water, fuel, supplies, and construction capability.

[S5] NASA, “Lunar Surface Technology”.

NASA identifies ISRU, excavation, infrastructure construction, power, robotics, and autonomy as key lunar capabilities.

Tesla’s first CIO describes building the custom Warp enterprise system in roughly four months in 2012 after rejecting off-the-shelf ERP, and its continuous extension thereafter.

Documents SpaceX’s internal Warp Drive enterprise and manufacturing systems.

Parameter literature

[S18] D. C. Jordan, S. R. Kurtz, K. VanSant, and J. Newmiller, “Compendium of Photovoltaic Degradation Rates”, Progress in Photovoltaics 24(7), pp. 978–989, 2016.

Meta-study of more than 11,000 measured degradation rates; terrestrial crystalline-silicon median approximately 0.5–0.6% per year.

[S19] W. Q. Lohmeyer, R. J. Aniceto, K. Cahoy, and A. Carlton, “Solar array degradation on geostationary communications satellites: the quantification of annual degradation and degradation over solar proton events”, International Journal of Space Science and Engineering 5(1), pp. 61–81, 2018.

Reported degradation ranges are approximately 0.44–1.03% per year for gallium-arsenide arrays and 0.71–1.69% for silicon arrays. This anchors one component class, not system-wide industrial depreciation.

[S20] S. Philipps and W. Warmuth, Fraunhofer ISE, Photovoltaics Report, July 14, 2026, p. 8; K. P. Bhandari et al., “Energy pay-back time and carbon footprint of commercial photovoltaic systems”, Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews 47, pp. 133–141, 2015.

Energy-payback estimates of roughly 0.9–1.1 years in Europe and a harmonized 1.0–4.1-year range across technologies. These do not measure reproduction of the production system.

[S21] M. Hecht, J. Hoffman et al., MOXIE results, Science Advances, 2022; D. L. Linne, G. B. Sanders, and K. M. Taminger, “Capability and Technology Performance Goals for the Next Step in Affordable Human Exploration of Space”, AIAA 2015-1650, pp. 8–9 and Table VI, also NASA NTRS 20150011681.

Oxygen produced on Mars at gram-per-hour scale at at least 98% purity; lunar oxygen extraction demonstrated at approximately 20% yield and TRL 5/6. Neither is a full-system closure demonstration.

[S22] Independent satellite tracking and reporting by J. McDowell, Harvard-Smithsonian CfA, 2020–2026.

Constellation deorbit and status statistics. Reported fractions near 3% for early generations fall below 0.5% for later ones, and the tracker separates early deorbit, uncontrolled decay, retirement, and disposal. Without cohort, observation interval, and satellite-years, these are fleet fractions rather than hazard rates.

Closure-engineering literature

[S23] NASA, Advanced Automation for Space Missions (NASA CP-2255), 1980 NASA/ASEE summer study; matter-closure and residual-import statements at sec. 5.3.6, report p. 219 (PDF p. 225).

Designs a proof-of-principle self-replicating lunar factory from a roughly 100-ton seed. It adopts a one-year strawman replication target whose component values it calls crude estimates; cites 90–96% closure from earlier studies of specific nonreplicating production applications; and places rigorous demonstration of complete parts closure outside its scope. These are design assumptions and plausibility arguments, not demonstrated performance.

[S24] R. A. Freitas Jr. and R. C. Merkle, Kinematic Self-Replicating Machines, Landes Bioscience, 2004.

Comprehensive survey of the design space for physical self-replicating systems.

Economics and progress-rate literature

[S25] R. H. Coase, “The Nature of the Firm,” Economica 4(16), 1937.

Transaction-cost account of firm boundaries used in II.5’s integration-versus-modularity analysis.

[S26] Epoch AI (Ho et al.), “Algorithmic Progress in Language Models,” 2024.

Estimates that compute required for fixed language-model performance halves roughly every eight months. The resulting approximately threefold-per-year rate does not license extrapolation to autonomous research or physical productivity.

Manyika (Google), “Towards a future space-based, highly scalable AI infrastructure system design,” arXiv:2511.19468 (v1 November 22, 2025; v2 June 17, 2026, the version carrying the detailed figures cited here), with the Project Suncatcher blog post.

Technical design study for satellite accelerator clusters: 67 MeV proton-beam testing of a Trillium TPU v6e, with HBM most TID-sensitive (irregularities from 2 krad(Si) against a 750 rad(Si) five-year requirement, no hard TID failures to 15 krad(Si)) and core logic/on-chip SRAM most SEE-sensitive; an inference error estimate near one per 3×10⁶ inferences under stated assumptions, with training impact reserved; an 81-satellite, 1 km-radius cluster near 650 km in dawn-dusk sun-synchronous orbit; and 800 Gbps unidirectional optical links against a roughly 10 Tbps per-link requirement. The authors twice state that the cost section is not a full economic analysis: it compares amortized launch cost per kW-year ($810 for a Starlink-v2-class ratio and $810–7,500 across classes at $200/kg) with terrestrial electricity spend ($570–3,000/kW-year), excluding buildings, infrastructure, and chips. Reaching approximately $200/kg by 2035 requires about 370,000 tonnes of additional cumulative launch mass, or roughly 1,800 Starship-class flights averaging 180 per year. Thermal management, ground communications, reliability, and repair remain open; orbital repair is described as impracticable and redundant provisioning proposed instead.

[S33] SpaceNews, Via Satellite, and Data Center Dynamics coverage of orbital-compute programs, 2025–2026.

Reports the Google–Planet partnership, two prototype satellites slated for launch by early 2027, the research-stage status of the program, and at least one additional entrant flying an accelerator demonstrator.

[S34] Will Marshall, co-founder and CEO of Planet Labs, interviewed on the Moonshots podcast with P. Diamandis and colleagues, episode 266, published June 26, 2026. A transcript with paragraph timestamps is archived at docs/transcripts/moonshots-266-2026-06-26.md.

Cited for mechanisms rather than measurements: launch tax versus compute tax (0:00:22 and 1:17:49); matching low-orbit decay life to hardware obsolescence; payload cost-performance outpacing launch cost-performance; limits on reproducing historical archives; finite compute-demand possibility; the protect-the-biosphere telos; and the recollected Google/Planet $200–300/kg crossover study (0:52:07). Recollections and projections are unverified.
