Contextual engineering and reporting sources

[S36] Assorted company disclosures, industry reporting, agency guidance, price sheets, and technical literature used to bound Appendix A and Part II scenarios.

Covers evidence not carried by [S18–S23]: foundry equipment-depreciation schedules (2–5 years); data-center accelerator retirement practice (3–6 years); a large-training-run disclosure of roughly 419 interruptions over 54 days across approximately 16,000 accelerators (cluster interruption frequency, not component hazard); 2019 reporting on factory construction cadence; 2026 humanoid-robot production targets; NASA small-spacecraft guidance on altitude-, ballistic-coefficient-, and solar-activity-dependent decay; launch price sheets; flexible-array and deployable-radiator performance; accelerator system pricing; AI-optimized data-center capex and PUE; and nuclear-restart PPA reporting. No single permanent identifier covers the collection. The r4.0 claim-level audit therefore does not use [S36] to justify any non-ASSUMPTION model endpoint. Ranges synthesized from these materials remain explicitly ASSUMPTION; [S36] supplies contextual bounds only. Every retained non-assumption endpoint instead has an exact record in params/claim_provenance.yaml.

[S37] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., European Union Prospectus, approved by BaFin, June 5, 2026, pp. 63, 70–72, 80–82, 97, and 137; see also the June 4, 2026 SEC-filed roadshow materials.

Primary company disclosure for the Starship aspiration normalization. It states that fully reusable Starship V3 is expected to carry 100 metric tonnes to orbit, that future generations could reach 200 tonnes potentially as soon as V4, and that Starship is intended eventually to reduce a cited historical $18,500/kg launch-cost benchmark by 99% or more. The resulting ≤$185/kg figure is arithmetic, not a quoted V3/V4 customer price. The $100/kg and $30–50/kg cases in Part II are progressively more aggressive sensitivity axes and are not attributed to this source. The prospectus also uses 100 kW/t to describe a long-term path to 100 GW of orbital AI-compute power per year—about one million tonnes and thousands of launches annually—and identifies full rapid reuse, approvals, spectrum, and long-duration reliability as dependencies. It warns that terrestrial energy improvements could diminish orbital viability. The target extraction and arithmetic are archived in docs/sources/spacex-ai-aspirations-2026-06.md.

[S38] Space Exploration Technologies Corp., Starmind AI1 official product page, accessed July 27, 2026; numeric provenance snapshot archived at docs/sources/starmind-ai1-2026-07-27.md.

First-party architecture disclosure for a planned orbital AI satellite: 150 kW peak / 120 kW average compute payload, 70 kW/tonne vehicle efficiency, 150 kW solar array at 250 W/m², 110 m² deployable liquid radiator, and a 20 m by 70 m deployed envelope. It also describes redundant pumped loops, debris shielding, laser links through Starlink, and sun-synchronous operation, but does not disclose vehicle capex, component mass, achieved availability, service life, qualification cost, or link cost. Company specification, not demonstrated performance.

Post-IPO orbital-compute calibration

[S39] S. G. Turyshev, “Orbital Data Centers: Spacecraft Constraints and Economic Viability”, arXiv:2604.27197, submitted April 29, 2026. The values used across [S39–S44] are consolidated in docs/sources/orbital-compute-calibration-2026-07-27.md.

Independent system-level closure across power, eclipse storage, thermal rejection, spacecraft fixed mass, communication intensity, utilization, finite life, and economics. Its representative 1 MW high-sunlight case requires 5,640 m² of BOL PV, 2,500 m² of radiator, 29.4 kg/kW for PV, storage, and radiators, and 34–59 kg/kW total after fixed spacecraft functions. At 40 kg/kW, $10,000–40,000/kW of terrestrial infrastructure permits only $250–1,000/kg for launch and spacecraft build combined before communications, operations, utilization, and life penalties. The paper’s annual-hazard penalties are illustrative sensitivities, not fleet measurements.

[S40] S. Gaalema, S. Indyk, and C. Staley, “Reduced-Mass Orbital AI Inference via Integrated Solar, Compute, and Radiator Panels”, arXiv:2604.07760, April 2026; and I. Bargatin, D. Jin, Z. Alansari, and J. R. Raney, “Tether-Based Architecture for Solar-Powered Orbital AI Data Centers”, arXiv:2512.09044 and AIAA SciTech 2026.

Low-mass inference architecture studies. The first reports a design basis above 100 kW/t using integrated PV, vapor-chamber radiators, and custom accelerators in a kilometer-scale array; its large example is about 150 tonnes and 16 MW. The second proposes 2–20 MW tethered systems with approximately 10 kg, 2 kW nodes. Both make mass-reducing integration assumptions whose deployment, dynamics, thermal, shielding, qualification, and lifetime closure remains prospective.

[S41] K. van Berkel, “The Cost and Network Limits of Space-Based AI Compute”, arXiv:2607.14172, submitted July 15, 2026.

Post-IPO compute-network comparison. For the modeled 8,000-accelerator systems, the terrestrial Clos fabric has 28,800 TB/s bisection bandwidth versus 2.25 TB/s for a two-dimensional and 10 TB/s for a three-dimensional orbital mesh at 100 Gbps links; estimated network latency is 150–450 times higher. The paper finds orbital inference potentially feasible but frontier LLM training uncompetitive on the analyzed meshes. Its aggressive $/kg and kg/kW economic premises are used here only as context; the network calculation is the calibration result.

[S42] R. Eason, N. Bleier, M. Lembeck, and R. Kumar, “Architecting Space Microdatacenters: A System-level Approach”, IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture, 2025.

Peer-reviewed cost/performance study of bespoke 0.5–10 kW microdatacenters for space-native workloads. Power and thermal functions account for roughly a third of modeled spacecraft TCO, compute hardware can be less than one percent, and energy-efficiency improvements are up to 2.5 times more valuable in space and reduce modeled TCO by approximately two-thirds. Its scale and in-orbit data origin differ from the Part II terrestrial-substitution case.

[S43] NASA Glenn Research Center, NASA/TM—2005-213442, radiator mass comparison, 2005.

Primary engineering reference separating radiator panels from the complete heat-transport and deployment system. ISS two-sided panels are reported at 2.75 kg/m² and 8.8 kg/m² after fluid loop and deployment mechanism; the JIMO analysis estimated 5 kg/m² for the complete system. At 353 K, 0.86 emissivity, and 173 K environment, the sizing example uses approximately 1.4 m²/kW. These are heritage/system cross-checks, not forecasts for an optimized AI1 radiator.

[S44] University of Virginia National Security Data Policy Institute, “Evaluating Space-Based Data Center Architectures: Capabilities, Constraints, and Trade-Offs”, Product No. 00036, May 19, 2026.

Policy synthesis with a simplified public cost model. Its representative five-year 1 GW estimates are $135.6 billion orbital versus $16.6 billion terrestrial under present-style assumptions, and $15.4 billion orbital only when launch falls to $30/kg, satellite hardware to $10/W, specific power rises to 100 W/kg, sunlight availability to 80%, and annual degradation and GPU failures each fall to 1%. It excludes GPU hardware, financing, insurance, logistics overhead, and downtime, so it is used only as a directional joint-condition check.

Lunar surface–orbit architecture and debris boundary

[S45] D. J. Kessler and B. G. Cour-Palais, “Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt”, Journal of Geophysical Research 83(A6), 2637–2646, 1978.

The original collision-feedback result: satellite collisions create orbiting fragments, each of which raises the probability of later collisions. It supplies the direction of the feedback, not a universal threshold for a particular future constellation.

[S46] N. R. Boone and R. A. Bettinger, “Simulation of Debris Events in Selected Low Lunar Orbits”, Journal of the Astronautical Sciences 70, 16 (2023).

Approximately 97,000 simulated fragments across eight breakup cases show orbit-dependent debris evolution: some selected low lunar orbits retain long-lasting populations, while impacts on the Moon are geographically nonuniform. The reported one-year collision probabilities are low for the notional present cases; the paper does not establish a current lunar cascade.

[S47] NASA, “Artemis Base Camp on the Moon Will Need Light, Water, Elevation”, 2021; NASA, “Lunar Dust Mitigation: A Guide and Reference”, 2021; and NASA, “Archway for Radiation and Micrometeorite Occurrence Resistance”, 2013.

Surface-architecture boundary references: south-polar illumination and access to shadowed volatile deposits; abrasive/electrostatic dust effects on radiators, mechanisms, and sensors; and local regolith as candidate bulk radiation and micrometeoroid shielding. None establishes reserve economics, continuous power at a selected site, or industrial closure.

[S48] D. C. Davis, F. S. Khoury, K. C. Howell, and D. J. Sweeney, “Phase Control and Eclipse Avoidance in Near Rectilinear Halo Orbits”, AAS Guidance, Navigation and Control Conference, 2020.

The Gateway reference NRHO is designed around eclipse avoidance, resonance, and low-cost stationkeeping with active phase control. It supports the gateway/service-layer role but does not make NRHO a passive, resource-bearing industrial site.

[S49] NASA, “Basics of Space Flight: Planetary Orbits”, updated 2024.

Defines a Sun-synchronous orbit as a planet-centered precessing orbit that preserves local solar time and distinguishes it from a heliocentric orbit around the Sun.

Orbital-data-center regulatory record

[S50] Federal Communications Commission, Space Bureau, “Space Bureau Accepts for Filing SpaceX’s Application for Orbital Data Centers”, Public Notice DA 26-113, released February 4, 2026; ICFS File No. SAT-LOA-20260108-00016, Call Sign S00798, application filed January 30, 2026.

The notice accepts for filing an application describing a non-geostationary system of up to one million satellites. Acceptance for filing begins public and regulatory review; it is not authorization to deploy or operate the proposed system.

Integrated bootstrap and material-source record

[S51] NASA Science, “Moon Composition & Structure”, updated July 23, 2026.

NASA lists oxygen, silicon, magnesium, iron, calcium, and aluminum as the principal elements in lunar-crust minerals, with smaller titanium, uranium, thorium, potassium, and hydrogen, and distinguishes calcium/aluminum-rich highlands from iron/titanium-rich maria. This is a bulk-composition boundary, not a resource or reserve estimate.

[S52] Jennifer Edmonson and Doug Rickman, “A Survey of Geologic Resources”, NASA Technical Reports Server record 20120015479, 2012.

The lunar-geology survey gives an average regolith bulk density of about 1.5 g/cm³ (1.5 t/m³), used only for the illustrative in-place inventory calculation in I.9. Density does not determine grade, recovery, or reserve economics.

[S53] P. G. Lucey, G. J. Taylor, and E. Malaret, “Abundance and Distribution of Iron on the Moon”, Science 268(5214), 1150–1153, 1995.

Near-global Clementine data produced an approximately 3 wt% iron estimate for the lunar highlands crust and approximately 7–8 wt% for lower-crustal material exposed by South Pole–Aitken. The 3% value is used as a conservative illustrative concentration, not a claim about a selected mining site.

[S54] C. B. Moore, C. F. Lewis, E. K. Gibson, and W. Nichiporuk, “Total Carbon and Nitrogen Abundances in Lunar Samples”, Science 167(3918), 495–497, 1970.

Returned bulk fines in the reported samples contained carbon and nitrogen at roughly hundreds of parts per million, with mixtures of indigenous, meteoritic, and solar-wind contributions. The result establishes scarcity in those samples, not a global lunar resource map.

[S55] NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, “NASA’s LRO: Lunar Ice Deposits Are Widespread”, October 3, 2024.

LRO analysis finds widespread evidence of water ice in permanently shadowed regions beyond the immediate south pole while explicitly stating that deposit volume and burial beneath dry regolith cannot yet be accurately determined. Occurrence is not a bankable reserve.

[S56] NASA Science, “OSIRIS-REx Frequently Asked Questions”, accessed July 27, 2026.

Laboratory analysis of returned Bennu material reports abundant organic molecules and sodium-rich minerals associated with evaporation of water. One carbonaceous sample demonstrates possible volatile and carbon-bearing diversity; it does not establish asteroid-mining yield or economics.

[S57] NASA, “Lunar Surface Technology”, accessed July 27, 2026.

NASA describes Blue Alchemist’s integrated autonomous processing of regolith simulant into silicon solar cells, aluminum wires, oxygen, iron, and slag; it also reports vacuum extraction of oxygen from simulant by a molten-regolith-electrolysis reactor. These are subsystem and prototype demonstrations, not autonomous lunar industrial closure.
